Literally, in every step of the experience (from drinks, to apps to entrees) we were the recipients of a screw up. It was like we were being punked! First, one waitress served the entire busy dining area, and though she tried her best, they definitely needed another server. Second, we struck out every step of the way when it came to ordering. Lastly, they need a new chef, pronto. The debacle began when I asked about the description about a beer special. The one served to me was a sour ale- not at all what was described- and I couldn't drink it. The waitress apologized, took it back and returned with a "safe bet". Minor hick-up. We ordered mussles in a white wine sauce, then asked about the dinner specials. My boyfriend ordered the Asian Bass w/ a red sauce and I had shrimp diablo. The mussles smelled great, but was inedible b/c it was way too salty. It tasted like the chef poured garlic salt into it, so we sent it back after 2 bites. I felt like i had a salt slick in my mouth the entire next day- it was that bad! When our entrees came out, turns out the waitress ordered my boyfriend the wrong item, even though he asked questions about the Asian Bass. She apologized, said she got confused (a testament to how frazzled she was). Mistakes happen; that's life. My boyfriend ate bread while they quickly rushed out his meal, which meant that I couldn't fully enjoy my dinner since I felt so bad for him. Finally- his dinner arrived, and low and behold- turns out "Asian Bass" meant it was battered and deep fried! Mind you, the description didn't state anything being friend, and he even asked the waitress to describe it, who omitted that part. Since he doesn't like anything tempura, to say he was disappointed was an understatement. At this point though, we were tired of complaining and just wanted to get our bellies full and get out of there. He said the Bass, once he scrapped the breading off , was delicious, thankfully. The flourless chocolate cake dessert was absolutely delicious, which we felt may be the only thing redeeming for the chef, but alas- turns out it was store bought. In hindsight, if the waitress hadn't been so busy, she should have offered us a complimentary dessert for our string of mishaps. Oh well, we just won't be going back for dinner anytime soon.

My friend had her chaise fully reclined and had been snoozing until this woke her up. 4) Bathrooms at the pool: were a mess, paper towels, toilet paper on the floor, water on the counters. The bathrooms shouldn't look so messy at a place where you are paying $700 a night. if the pool staff went thru here every 30 minutes to ck on it this could be kept from happening, but they don't act like they do team service or are thinking past where their next tip comes from. 5) Room service - the food was pretty good, the servers were very nice, but for 2 of our meals items were forgotten 1) we asked for ranch dressing w/ our fries and it didn't come. I never got a call back so called the next am since we were cking out that day. they called me later in the morning and said I could pick up what I had left from the pool bar. text: FRIDAY BRUNCH What can be more fun than dressing in your Sunday best, standing in line along filthy Bourbon street, and feeling the excitement of Friday brunch at Galatoire's? We always get there early and tip, to ensure that we get seated in the coveted downstairs dinning room. Then while we wait, we enjoy a milk punch upstairs and just marvel in the atmosphere. Friends and family hugging and screaming like they hadn't seen each other in ages. Gaggles of older women huddled up eying the new bride, who is twenty years younger then her new groom. Teenagers conspiring to get some alcoholic beverages of their own. I love it all. It only gets better when you get seated downstairs and enjoy the BEST service in New Orleans. From the way they stream the pot of scalded milk and the pot of chicory coffee together into my cup to make an au lait, to the intimate and personal knowledge they have of the menu and their recommendations, these servers are wonderful! The dinning room is loud, and filled with giant hats and families that have been coming here for generations. The food is old school New Orleans and some of the best you can find in the city. But the best part of it all, is the experience. I'm sure you can go to Galatoire's any time and have a good meal. However, do yourself a favor and go on Friday with the locals. Get their early and you wont regret it.

text: Heard about Elizabeths being a great place for food, figured pizza is in the name so that was the thing to go with. Got some take out pizzas for a trail and review. First the pizzas are a bit on the smaller size when you consider the usual size of pizzas from local establishments and chains. They come in 2 sizes with various options. Got a mini (4 slices) with the white crust, tomato sauce, mozzarella cheese, and pepperoni. The pepperoni was thinly slices and mild. There was some spice to it, but not much. Fairly standard pizza and didn't really stand out to me. The crust is a thin style but well cooked in the oven, tasted like a brick oven firing. The regular size pizza i got (10 inches) with some custom topping was a bit better. The honey wheat bread, the sign says flour ground by them, was okay. The problem is that with the very thin crust and other toppings there was very little difference to me between the standard white versus the wheat crust in taste or mouth feel. The chunky tomato sauce was a very good upgrade. There are small pieces of soft tomato flesh in the sauce with a bright and tangy tomato taste. Once of the better sauces I have had recently. The country sausage was a bit one dimensional with limited flavors. The rosemary sauteed onions were also a bit one dimensional. I did not find the onions to impart much of a flavor compared to a plain sauteed onion. Overall the pizza was okay, the only thing that stood out in my meal was the chunky tomato sauce. Otherwise I have had better crusts and better toppings elsewhere for less cost. Perhaps the restaurant menu and entrees are better, but I am not hopeful since "pizza" is in their title and should be their signature dish. I would rather go elsewhere, have better pizza, and spend less.

The server took our drink order, but my friend who ordered the sangria had to wait until the rest of us were almost done with our drinks even though the pitcher of sangria was sitting right on the bar. Two of our entrees were served and we waited for the other two until our friends told us to eat while the food was still warm. We were just about finished when the other two dishes showed up. The server never apologized or explained what was going on. She sat behind the bar and sipped on her drink as if she was a customer instead of an employee. Given the tab was almost $100, I expect better food and a lot better service. This was the worst restaurant I've been to in SB or anywhere else for that matter.

text: Believe the hype! Were it not for the interminable wait to get a table (almost two hours), I would give it 5 stars. Once in, the service was great. We ordered the regular burger and the whisky king. Forget about the regular burger. The whisky king is pricy but ABSOLUTELY worth it. I don't know what kind of voodoo magic they use to make this burger so delicious. The burger meat is juicy and cooked all the way through evenly, the bacon is perfection and the piece of foie gras was almost half as big as the burger. I can't wait to go back to Philadelphia to eat that burger again. Skip the cheddar fries and the short rib cheddar fries. They are ok, but not fantastic. Save yourself for the whisky king alone, you won't be disappointed. Have drinks at Tinto while you wait and assume that an hour wait really is two hours.

text: I read about this place in the Inquirer years ago in a piece about the best steaks in the area, and if I remember correctly, this place won. For some strange reason, I woke up about 8PM today from a nap craving a cheese steak and my mind darted to Leo's after God knows how much time since I last thought about it. So I jumped in the car and took a drive down (from University City). Nice mom-and-pop feel and convenient to supplementary stores (Wawa, dairy drive-through). I gotta have my Wawa 1/2gal tea. The large steaks are HUGE. Longer than my forearm (including my hand) and I'm a pretty large guy, and thicker than a tuna can around. You're paying for that too, they're about $12 a piece, but considering they're about as long as (or maybe a bit longer) than 2 you'd get anywhere else, and packed MUCH more than any other place, it's about right. Pretty good. Ingredients were well above average (loved the cheese). I'm not going to say its the best I've had, but its up there. I probably should have asked for a dash of salt. All-in-all pretty darn good. Not worth another drive all the way down past the Sunoco refinery and the airport just for a steak, but worth stopping for if in the area. Yes I finished it (after a couple 5-10 minute breaks toward the end) and I was near-bursting.

text: I hate to be a downer, but maybe Anthony's lost his edge since the last time someone reviewed him. I made a Friday after-work appointment, and my first red flag was getting a call in the morning to ask if I could come in an hour earlier instead. Since I had specifically made the appointment at that time precisely because I would still be working, I explained that unfortunately I wouldn't be able to come in that early, but I'd do my best to get in as early as possible. Turns out I got off work earlier than usual that day, and I was in 20min before my scheduled appointment time. Anthony was waiting for me at the reception desk and whisked me off fast enough that I practically had to jog to catch up with him. He was personable enough while he was doing the waxing, but I could tell he really wanted to be out of there ASAP. Also, he waxed my hair in really odd directions (horizontally across my lower leg), which would make sense if my hair grew like that, but it doesn't: it grows straight down, so he was waxing sideways against the grain and, in some places, with the grain. It hurt a little more than usual, but that could just be me, so that's not the issue. When he was done he zipped out of the room and the second I had the door open he was going in with a male customer, with whom he was much more chatty than he'd been with me. I didn't even get a "bye" and saw myself to the desk to pay, where I left a 20% tip. Then I got home and actually looked at my legs. Stubbly. PATCHY. Horrible. Look, I know a whole leg wax is a long and fairly tedious task, but that's why it costs more. This was a terrible wax job: I have patches of hair on my left knee, left lower leg on both sides of my calf, all over my left thigh, back and side of my right knee, top of my right thigh. He also left wax residue on several large areas, which is just sloppy, but that washes off. The patches of hair don't. What did I pay for if not for hair removal? Even worse, when I run my hand up against the grain of my hair growth, I can feel the stubble. He BROKE OFF the hair on almost all of the area he waxed instead of pulling it out. No, it isn't just a matter of "oh, your hair's just growing at different cycles." It's evenly broken off. All over my legs. I uploaded a couple pictures; I have really light-colored coarse hair, but you can at least see part of the disaster on my left thigh relatively well. Avoid.

text: Let's just say that I have a hard time taking Tart L.'s reviews to heart (maybe thats just me?) but I am glad that I listened and stopped by Yanni's today. We went for a lateish Sunday lunch. It wasn't crowded and service was great. Yanni himself came out of the kitchen numerous times to make sure everything was okay and to "toot his own horn" by claiming that it was "the best Greek food in the city". And he's not lying. When we decided to stop in I was imagining a lunch of falafel and hummus, neither of which can be found on Yanni's menu. Let's just say that they were not missed. We started with an appetizer of (vegetarian) rice stuffed grape leaves ( or dolmadakia ) and some of the best, freshest pita I have ever tasted. I followed that by the Spanakopita and mini Greek salad. The spinach was perfectly cooked, it wasn't too cheesy, and the pastry was divine. The salad went with it very nicely. I practically licked my plate clean. There are actually a lot of vegetarian items on the menu and even a decent vegan selection. Especially if you like eggplant. You can check out the menu on their website. On top of the food the place has a great little patio that is perfect on a nice warm autumnal day or for a romantic evening. Don't miss out on this great locally owned place! ( and rumor has it that Yanni also owns the Athens family restaurant so if you like that place but are looking for a little something "nicer" be sure and give this place a try!)

text: My husband tried to get me to MOVE to STL, so several visits to the city included a pit stop at Comfort Inn. Was he trying to sell me a city or a hotel, I'll never know, b/c this place was REALLY nice. It also is in a GREAT location, near everyone one might need and the very popular Westport Center which boasts tons of great eateries, bars and coffee joints. Speaking of price, it is super affordable, and we always got our king bed, nonsmoking room request. Wireless is free (big bonus) and it has a nice desk/sitting area where I could work (since I work from home, this is important when I travel). All the doors are on the inside (a must have for people who rarely leave the hotel), the maid service was fast, tidy and always left me extra towels (I am wasteful and enjoy two per shower - one for head, one for body and those small hand towels don't work for me). There is also a great restaurant connected to the hotel that delivers for a mere $2.00 per delivery (score another point for Comfort Inn Westport!). The food is good, hot and comes in less than hour. Are you Fellow Yelpers seeing that I am a big fat lazy ass on my weekend trips? I am...it's sad, I know, but these things MATTER to a girl like me. :) I say ...if you are not sure where to stay...Comfort Inn, is a great "home away from home". And, if you are wondering, we didn't end up moving, but if we did, I would need to find out the monthly rate of the Comfort Inn b/c it might be worth it!

text: I think McGurks is great for a few different crowds at different times of the day or week. So if you walk into Mcgurks during the day and you're there for lunch, you're going to find the atmosphere completely different than say 11pm on Saturday night. I prefer the daytime crowd during the week or weekends, but I'm also a bit older and don't care to stand around a bunch of loud people getting drunk anymore. There is certainly a great party crowd here on the weekends and I'm all about encouraging people looking for a good night out to stop in at Mcgurks while they are going through Soulard. For the daytime folks, and what the rest of my review will focus on, there is the daytime McGurks. I've got a few favorite plates: the wings, the chicken sandwiches (cajun and BBQ), spinach ravioli, and their burgers. Pub fare, I know, but I've found that they are consistent and it is always prepared just right. Their beer selection is good, and their cocktails are never lacking the right amount of kick. I like to go in for lunch occasionally and I also enjoy spending a Saturday or Sunday afternoon at one of their two outdoor bars in a very large and comfortable patio. I would say their patio is only second in size to Molly's, but I prefer McGurks' patio over Molly's from a service perpsective. So, in terms of service - again, for the daytime, I think they do a fantastic job. They have five bars, three inside and two outside, and their plentiful staff always does a good job of keeping drinks filled, food delivered on time, bills picked up when I'm ready, etc. All in all, McGurks has a lot for the different crowds and I always bring out of towners here to spend a meal or afternoon there. I'd say check it out - but know what you're looking for before showing up as the crowd varies as the hours wane.

text: Mimi's in the Marigny **** A GEM! I don't get why this place exists, because it is too good to be true. Good drinks with wonderful and authentic Spanish tapas; and all very reasonable. No tapas were more than $7.00! My Long Island...was only $6.00. Woa...I felt like I was robbing them. The vibe is very comfortable and bohemian. Dimly lit, and not sterile at all. Order the "Trust Me" item on the menu, and you will have the fortune of experiencing the free creativity of the chef. They simply make you what they want...and it is always well worth it. One of the dishes I got was this elegant tower of succulent prawns, layered with pickled avocado, a lump of fried goat cheese, fresh caviar, and lamb demi-glace. Every dish made me happy, it was such a dream come true (and a wonderfully flavorful escape from all that fried crap one finds in the rest of the city). Only complaints: more staff would be good. Service was a little slow. Wine was generally gross...go for the mixed drinks or beer instead. If I lived in the Marigny, I would soooooo be a regular here. To the chef: what you are doing is wonderful---Don't Stop! Mimi's was one of the most pleasant dining experiences I had while visiting the Big Easy. ---Anthony

text: This was my first apartment in Tucson. I didn't know any better then. There are a lot of car break-ins, but I never had any problems, possibly because I was driving such a beater at the time. I lived in a tiny studio with a bedroom area separated from the living area by a huge cabinet sort of thing that came with the apartment. Next to me was the guy who I could hear having sex at least three times per month (I would hope that he got more action than that though) and then bang on the wall when I played the stereo during the day, the other side was a creepy drunk redneck who would always try to talk to me, and below was a college kid who would have 100+ people parties spilling out of his 400sf apartment. Fun times at that Promontory! The managers were possibly the biggest jerks I've ever encountered in renting. I once turned in my rent check on the morning of the 2nd and was given a late charge of $35. I would complain about things and would mostly be ignored. The grounds are immaculately kept, likely in order to deceive you into thinking that this is actually a good place to live. There are tennis courts, pools (usually frequented by creepy guys) and on-site laundry, the latter of which is overpriced. It's nice that it's on a little street behind a strip mall and in a desert area, but there were always issues with getting out of there. For one, there was a traffic light at Stone and River that you could use, but people turning left from Stone onto River would always ignore the fact that you were there and there were quite few accidents as a result. The city finally changed the light to create a delay on the signal from Stone and that has alleviated the problem. Not sure if things have changed since I've lived there, but I really doubt it. I went up there about a year later to help a random son of a friend of a friend and tried to talk him out of it, but he said it was okay (but he also knew everything about anything, which was pretty amazing), and it actually looked a little worse. More shopping carts, more abandoned cars and people still flying through the ridiculously large parking lot. It's just better not to rent at a larger complex in Tucson unless you're absolutely sure that it's a good place. This one is definitely not one of those good places, and remains the second worst apartment complex I've lived in.

text: A friend and I went to the Roxy Bar this past Saturday before a show. Typically, I do not like eating and going to bars in the Reno casino's, as I am not a fan of second hand smoke. However, with it's quaint atmosphere and dark lighting I forgot that I was in the El Dorado Casino. The front part of the bar where we sat over looks the water fountains. Additionally, there are your typical round tables with tall chairs, large comfty chairs and a few normal height square tables. The tables and chairs face a grand piano and microphone, in which a piano player played and a singer sang while we were in the bar. The music was perfect and not overly loud as some bars and restaurants can be, where you can hardly hear what those at your table are saying. If you walk further into the bar, there is your typically bar seating facing the bartenders. Little did we know when we arrived at 5:00 (on a Saturday), Happy Hour was still taking place. 4:30-6:00 all martini's are $5.00. After 6, the martini's go back up to $9. In addition to the live jazz music, Roxy is known for their 101 martini's. I had a mojitomartini which tasted like a mojito, very fresh and light, and my friend had your typical martini with spicy olives. We also ordered the chicken skewer/rice appetizer for $7 which tasted much better than we were expecting. Your waitress/waiter will also bring a bowl of nuts if requested. Overall, a fun, relaxing bar to catch up with friends, enjoy a martini, and listen to live jazz music!

text: I've lived in the Philly area for 15 years and have been visiting Monk's since year one. I've been for lunch, dinner, happy hour, brunch, or just a quick beer in the middle of the afternoon. I think I'm qualified to comment about this place. I believe that Monk's success is due in large part to their ability to meet the needs of several audiences. Let me explain. The Beer Lovers- This is arguably the biggest group. Monk's is literally a legend in the beer world. Not just in Philly but across the country. Their beer list is superb. I once sat at the bar on a Saturday afternoon with a couple who had driven for hours from Maryland just for the beer. Not to have lunch. Not to visit the Philly historic sites. Just to drink beer at Monk's. The Mussel People- At the moment they have six flavors and people go crazy! I've seen tables where patrons order pots of all six. Trust me; these people are devoted to this place. The Foodies- You can be surprised here. How about "Monk's Flemish Grilled Scallops" as a starter? Follow it with Salmon Framboise and if you love seafood you have one heck of a meal. There are also plenty of choices for carnivores. If you are a newbie you may be a little surprised by the physical space. There is a short dingy hallway that leads from the street to the main door. The rooms are quirky, homey, and just a little bit beat up. It all adds to the famous Monk's charm! I'm sure I'll be back again and again for another 15 years!

text: As far as road trip breakfast options go, few places compare to Bob Evans. I must have been to this particular Bob Evans location at least 20 times. The food is always fresh, the service is always friendly and the place is always clean. For those of you on the West Coast who are not familiar with Bob Evans, let me introduce you. Bob Evans is a couple of steps above Denny's and Waffle House, a step above Marie Callender's and on par with Cracker Barrel. In fact, in my twisted pancake-and-syrup dreams, I like to imagine that Bob Evans is married to Marie Callender, because they're kind of similar in many ways. Denny's could be their son, and they could all live in a Waffle House down the street . . . Are you still reading, or have I lost you completely? Bob Evans markets simple, down-to-earth country fresh food. I recommend Bob Evans for breakfast. I tried it for lunch once, and I wasn't impressed. Eggs, bacon and pancakes are kind of difficult to mess up. I always opt for Farmer's Choice breakfast, which includes 2 pancakes, 3 strips of bacon, 2 eggs and some home fries for only $8.59 (prices and participation may vary). Add a cup of weak coffee, and you're looking at $10 + tip. It's fast, easy, convenient and, most importantly, fresh. Bob Evans' pancakes are very good, but their specialty is biscuits 'n' gravy. 2 biscuits and a bowl of rich, creamy gravy is a great unhealthy way to complement your great unhealthy meal. Strongly recommended. It's a chain, so the decor is consistent across all Bob Evans locations (and I'm not ashamed to say I've visited many of them from Indiana to Maryland and from Michigan to Florida). The decor is that of a mass-produced generic country house with light wood accents, rusty cans, Mason jars and checkered curtains. It doesn't make you feel at home, but it does make you feel welcome. When I embark on a road trip, I always plan to have breakfast at a Bob Evans or a Cracker Barrel. They offer way better options and way better service than most other roadside establishments.

text: I could not have had a more different experience than the other person who reviewed Pat's. I went here because it was close (I just moved to the area and the only person I know recommended a place in the city, which seemed inconvenient) and because I read the previous review. My car was running fine, for the most part, but as I was scheduled to take a trip in a week, I wanted to take care of one tiny problem- a low grumbling when I turned the car on in the morning- rather than risk it being exacerbated by my upcoming long drive. About 6 hours after I dropped it off, Pat called, telling me I needed almost $400 worth of repairs. I reluctantly agreed, thinking this kind-seeming, older man would not take advantage of me for my lack of knowledge about cars and/or, let's face it, my gender. He told me it would be ready the next day. The next day came and went, with no phone call from Pat. Next morning, around 9AM, Pat calls and tells me, oh yeah, I suddenly have a spike in my tire, it's now completely undriveable and a new tire is going to cost $80! For one tire! Forget the fact that he's had my car for an entire day with no contact, but he basically admitted that the flat happened in between my dropping off the car and his calling me two days later, after someone drove it around "diagnosing" the problem and determining the costly repairs I'd be paying for. So I go pick it up and another Pat at the desk tells me there is still something wrong with the car- one of the things I authorized them to fix over the phone the day before. Cue another Pat. This is the Pat I spoke to on the phone, who denies my telling him to go ahead and fix this particular problem. That will be an additional $240. He has the nerve to print me an estimate for this additional repair, inviting me to come back and have it fixed soon. Anyone who doesn't have the time or interest to devote themselves to learning the details of auto repair is at the mercy of the mechanic. It was my mistake choosing Pat's for the convenience of their location. Don't let it be yours. Let me save you the frustration. $400 and an exorbitant tire replacement later, you'll be kicking yourself just like I am.
label: NEG

text: This is a hidden gem, because itâs not much from the outside, or even from the inside. But the owner, Leah, welcomes you into her place like itâs her home. In an age where genuine human contact is increasingly rare, women like Leah can help but put a smile on your lips and feel a little lighter with whatever load youâre carrying. She welcomes you and thanks you for coming, and in between, sheâs eager to find out what she can get you, and doesnât speak to you like a customer, but like another human being. The day I came in she was lounging around with two of her elderly guests, talking to them like family. There are some couches amid the tables and chairs and the places has been decorated with Caribbean decor. It feels homey and festive. I went to pay for my freshly brewed coffee and cinnamon bun and realized it was cash only. I asked her if there was a bank machine close by. She said not to worry but to sit down and enjoy my coffee, Then when I was done sheâd tell me where to find a bank machine. When I was done, she simply said. Come again and pay next time. text: I've been a member of this gym for seven months and I really enjoy it. I don't think it's totally fair to rate a place based on the clientele, and at any gym you are likely to run into a crowd looking for bootay rather than a good workout. That said, I think the ratio of your average gym enthusiasts to date-hunters is perfectly acceptable. You also have your share of juice-heads and eating disordered gals, but again, it comes with the territory. I base whether or not I like a gym mostly on how often their personal trainers bother me. Aside from the occasional "hello," "have a nice day" or smile, they leave me alone. I also feel like when and if I have a question, they will nicely answer me and know what they're talking about. There is a good selection of weight machines and free weights and tons of cardio machines. I've stuck to the elliptical, treadmill, and weights but I would like to pick up a class soon. Which leads me to my only real complaint: a large portion of the classes that I'm interested in taking are held during the day. I run into that with many gyms though. I like that Bally feels like less of a Wal-Mart of Gyms like LA Fitness, but has more to offer in the way of equipment and a knowledgeable staff than your neighborhood YMCA. The Foothills location offers killer deals all the time too, so go in and see what they can offer you instead of buying online like I did. A few weeks ago they offered membership for $13.86 a month!

text: I was in Royersford earlier today with about 45 minutes to kill and an empty tummy that required filling. I waved the white flag and began to pull into a fast food joint, when I spied the Palermo's sign. Now, I've been a regular customer of the Palermo's in Center Square for years and years, and while I vaguely knew they had other locations I never came across them. I just assumed they didn't really exist. But...there it was! I could not resist. My immediate impression was "wow...this is much bigger, newer, and nicer than the "real" Palermo's". All true, as this location was probably a field, or forest, or something 5-10 years ago. I love the "real" Palermo's but the parking sucks, its cramped, etc...none of that applied here. Sure, you trade some "charm" for such modern conveniences but I was in no mood to quibble...I was in a mood to nibble (sorry). There are two things I get at Palermo's...pizza (duh) and falafel. Both on the menu here, but I went with the pizza in order to make my comparison. Service was very friendly and like the Center Square location you pay after you eat, even though its counter service. A slice of cheese and a slice of white with ricotta and tomato were served hot and ready to roll (and by that, I mean fold). Honestly, if I didn't know better, I'd think I got a slice from the "real" Palermo's. Just as good in every way. Best pizza sauce anywhere within a half days drive of Philly. Crusty crust where it matters, just thin enough to hold it together everywhere else but gives a nice "snap" when folded. Yea, yea, Old Forge, North Jerz, whatever...I'm not driving there just to get pizza. It is not the cheapest slice you can find but it is the best. I've had pizza from other places in RoFo over the years and they can't touch Palermo's. Just don't bother. Eat here or starve to death...any other choice is fallacy.
label: POS

Slippery use of statistics in the recent piece on Nashville police crime-reduction strategies is a good example. The Scene is also not shy about tearing people in the community apart in really brutal ways... most of the time their targets deserve it, but sometimes the pieces that center on individuals are over-the-top and seem to leave out any details that might make us more sympathetic to the bad guy or girl.

text: This is the first review of a restaurant I have ever written and I live in 'gourmet ghetto' Berkeley. We were passing through Reno on the way home from Burning Man and happened across Naan and Kabab. Maybe it's just that we were starving for something besides granola and beef jerky, but I don't think so - this restaurant is outstanding. To start, it's small, cozy, with colorful and creative decor, great service, and Maurice, the chef, is friendly and available for questions. The food came quite quickly given that it's made to order, everything was very fresh, including the tasty salad. It seems lately to be the trend to make fabulous food, beautifully arranged....in very small quantities - but Naan and Kabob served sumptuous, large quantities, and made it beautiful on the plate, as well. We had a Gyros Plate and a Mediterranean Steak, both delicious and reasonably priced. It's easily accessible from I80 and really worth stopping if you are travelling through. If you live in Reno, you're lucky to have Naan and Kabab!

text: Our family celebrated the 4th of July by driving down to see the family in Southern California for a quick hi-bye visit. On our way back up the coast, we stopped in Santa Barbara for brunch. We decided NOT to yelp a place or to over-plan, and so we just drove along until we found Jeannine's . . . pulling (an illegal) U-turn to snag a spot right in front of the shop. After a quick perusal of the specials on the white board right outside on the balcony, I made my decision on breakfast -- salmon benedict (who counts calories on the 4th?). We inched our way into the store to place our order, since this is an order at the counter and they'll deliver your order kind of a place. I was very happy to see the sign "Proudly serving Peet's Coffee" and to taste that the coffee was correctly brewed fresh and strong (and very happy that it was unlimited refills -- serving Major Dickerson and a French Roast -- and a decaf variety that I honestly didn't even really notice). My brunch selection was delightful, with the egg poached to perfect done-ness -- still oozie-but-mostly-set yolk, with the egg white perfectly finished off. The hollandaise sauce was very creamy and good; it was not too salty, which was good because smoked salmon is always flavorful, and the pairing would have been too much if the hollandaise sauce was of normal saltiness. The potatoes were a mix of purple and "regular" potatoes and nicely seasoned. My kids and husband enjoyed their food, as well. So, so far, this would have been a solid FOUR STAR experience. What set it over the top was the hot chocolate art. Check out the photo and the care that they gave on the foam art! This cheery sight was enough to nudge my boy out of his little morning funk, and what mom wouldn't appreciate this joyful milk wink? The special service and attention at Jeannine's is what gives them that extra star. From the barista to the waiter to the busboy, every staff here was enjoying their day and going above-and-beyond to ensure a great experience.
label: POS

text: Stonewood prides itself as an upscale, dinner-only restaurant experience..a bad experience I would have to add. I've been there twice in the past two weeks. Both times the service had been sub-par, which is appalling for a restaurant that dares to call itself "upscale". The waiters are horrible actors, showing a fake kind of politeness to their customers, while still expected a hefty tip once the meal is complete, and that would be a LARGE tip considering the prices of their meals. The meals are like an appetizer at Ruby Tuesday, and don't taste much better than the Olive Garden, for double and sometimes TRIPLE the prices. I've had their Oak Grilled Burger, which had no real taste to it. Compare to the Cheesecake Factory, a real upscale restaurants, Kobe Burger that has a taste in the beef that just oozes out into your mouth without needing to add condiments and you find yourself with a DRY burger that tastes like cooked paper. Condiments are highly needed just to give it some kind of substance. In addition the french fries were horrible, I'd rather have McDonald's, Checkers, or dare i say it, BURGER KING (the most horrible french fry dealer on Earth, now second to most horrible). They had tons of seasoning on them, but the seasoning was of no help to the bland taste that came with them. During my next visit for my Aunt's 35th birthday (someone explain to me why restaurants do so horrible with birthday dinners, where they get so much business from, are they just nervous, or just ignorant of the impression they are making on fairly large parties), I had a lobster ravioli meal with my mother. For twenty-two dollars, we received three (yes three), small raviolis with a small amount of lobster sauce on top, and a kabob with shrimp on it. Frankly, I could have had more food anywhere else I can think of in my head. Clearly making this restaurant a, I'm rich so I'm just going to blow all my money on AIR and dark lighting kind of restaurant. First of all, let me say that we had THREE waiters in the same night. The waiters had no clue what had gone on with the waiter before them, and I'm utterly shocked that we received our meals at all. They actually had us tell them what we had at the end so that they could bill us, it would have been so easy to lie and just pay a small price after they took all our plates away. It's not always to be so honest, but alas we were. I had to track the waiters down for refills. The cup size they give you is slightly bigger than a shot glass, and their food is DRY. It just doesn't make any sense. The waiters half the time seemed to just ignore my glares for them to come and pay attention to me, the person who is controlling their tip. Like I said, I do not understand any of it. The only good thing at this restaurant, saving it from the taboo of one star is their exquisite clam chowder. It tastes amazing, they have the best recipe I have ever had. If I could get the clam chowder, and ignore everything else, that would be swell. I have never eaten clam chowder so quickly and indulged so much into a soup like I did into theirs. They should add a bread bowl and I would be SET. If it were up to me, the waiters would have received nothing in tips and frankly I would have probably complained to no end to the management. Since I was in the party of others, the restaurant was saved of my fury. Of course, I can't let them off that easily. This restaurant is such a wreck that I'm going to give them suggestions to make it better. 1. Get bigger glasses for drinks or make your food more MOIST. There are just no excuses for this. 2. Either lower your prices or add more food, you charge more than the Cheesecake Factory, which is utterly superior to you in every single way. 3. Turn the lights up a little. I didn't see barely any couples there in both my visits, the tables are too big for couples, and you can barely see your own hands in that kind of darkness. Take a note from the Cheesecake Factory, they don't leave their customers blind in the darkness while trying to have conversations and eat their meals. 4. Fire or re-train all your waiters, they suck. They don't know how to attend to peoples needs. That is all. Until we meet again.
label: NEG

text: As a first time Southwest flyer I was very disappointed on the Detroit side. I flew on a "buddy pass" which is pretty much flying stand by. Since I had never flown this way before I was full of questions when my turn finally arrived at the check in counter (after a very lengthy line). Of course as soon as I made my way to the counter the man behind the counter disappeared. I tried to ask the lady at the next computer for help and she was very rude (I wish I had gotten her name)! Finally, she told me which option to choose & my security pass would print. Getting through security wasn't bad, moved fairly quick! Upon my arrival to my gate I was told that I would be called up 10 minutes before final board "if" there were any available seats by a not so friendly agent. text: Ahh, B.B's. Home to some of my favorite memories. As well as some of my favorite non-memories, if I'm to believe my friends when they tell me about the antics I got up to last night. (I personally, don't. And the goat doesn't, either.) Food - Try the sweet-potato fries, which are a meal unto themselves, given the gracious quantity they present you with. Or the shrimp po-boy; the house made remoulade is awesome sauce. Literally. Of course, if you're feeling more ambitious, any of the tantalizing specials they offer on a nightly basis are fair game. I dare you to try one and not like it. They also have some really good vegetarian options, for the meatless. Service - The bartenders are phenomenal. Rob, Sharon, Nick and Griffin are all personable, knowledgeable and most importantly, quick. This is important when you're being jostled about at the bar 10 minutes after last call and you want to squeeze in one last libation before heading to the East Side. Atmosphere - Warm woods surround the bar. Flattering lighting. Pictures of blues and jazz legends grace the walls. The whole space just screams, "Come in and get toasty and/or toasted!" On weeknights, you'll usually find a band of regulars enjoying the music. Come Friday and Saturday night, a decidedly younger, more party-hearty crowd comes in, especially after the 1:30 bars close. Music - The real reason people flock to B.B.'s. On a given night, you'll find a myriad of bands bringing down the house with authentic bluesy, jazzy, yummy goodness. No matter who they are, rest assured - they'll be good. More often than not, they'll be legendary. The staff (and owner, Mark O'Shaughnessy) wouldn't have it any other way. The shows are creative and dynamic, and always a surprise. It's incredibly common to see musicians show up, instruments in tow, and hop up on stage to play with their buddies for an impromptu jam session. It's the energy of the place, really. I don't know of any other bar where you can find a laid-back vibe paired with such a up atmosphere. The juxtaposition makes it great.

text: This was my second time at the steakhouse in the past two years, and I was surprised at how much the food had deteriorated. The first time, the place was not so busy and the meat was delicious. It revealed itself as what it really is: a big indifferent wildly overpriced cafeteria. I had three cuts of steak, and they were the fattiest pieces of meat I've ever encountered in a restaurant. Ghastly pieces of glistening gristle. I shrugged off the first piece -- shit happens -- but it was nasty. The second piece, however, was equally yellow and what little meat in it was stringy with fat and muscle. By the third piece,a 2-inch square of "garlic-flavored sirloin" -- gristle rolled in burnt garlic (blech!) --my stomach was beginning to roil as I gazed at the mounting plate of picked-apart blubber. My dinner companion thought I had to be exaggerating. He forked a piece of the "meat" from my plate and popped it into his mouth, at which point he got a funny sick look on his face for there he sat, his mouth full of nasty rubbery fat. He had a decision to make: eat his words or eat a big chunk of cellulite. Even though he hates to be wrong, and will eat nearly anything, he spit the fat out: it was that disgusting. My last attempt was a bit of parmesan-crusted pork tenderloin, which was dry but tasty and, praise be, trimmed of fat. However, by then my appetite and my patience were shot. All I could think of was that this festival of fat was going to cost me $50 plus $10 for a glass of cheap wine. And tip. All that for a tricked-out cafeteria. When the waiter brought the check I pointed to all the fat on my plate. He responded like a cafeteria clerk, noting in a flat voice that "some cuts of meat are fatty." Of course! That's why we trim them, pal, before charging people $50 for pieces of low-grade sirloin. Pony up for a ginsu knife and some quality control, Fatty de Chao! And for you carnivores: save your money and go to a cheap steakhouse, where the meat and the check won't make you sick to your stomach.

text: I was living in Philadelphia's riverfront when Cuba Libre first opened up and it was a blessing to the neighborhood. The neighborhood loved it, the tourists loved it, the beautiful people loved it. Then it got big and pretentious and it forgot its neighbors. Now it has transitioned into a mature restaurant, still with quality, but showing the mediocrity of a tired establishment. After a two year absence since I moved to DC, I went there and was pleased with some of its food, but virtually nothing else. It has gone a long way down from the outstanding restaurant I remember five years ago. First of all: I'm Cuban. I know my Cuban food. I can cook very good Cuban food, save for the tediously prepared food items such as "tostones" (or patacones in other Latin American countries), and the basic staples such as white rice that don't take any art in its manufacture. So as a result, I'm probably a little bit more critical, but that's because I know Cuban food quite well. I also know that a Cuban restaurant should have a much more welcoming attitude. What stroke my bad side was that the staff didn't seem to care. The espresso machine was down and all I was able to get was dish-water quality American coffee. Frankly, that's inexcusable at a Cuban restaurant. Get a backup. Get those little Italian stovetop machine my mom used to use. Whatever. A Cuban meal without Cuban coffee is like a German meal without schnitzel, or a French dinner without a Claret. The "guanábana" (soursop) juice was obviously a Goya $1.99 can of nectar with water added. We arrived at 1020 and were literally ignored outside of the restaurant until 1030. Not even an acknowledgement. At 1030, the maitre d' opened the door and ushered us in. We sat outside and had an attentive waiter who fortunately made up for the increasing shortcomings of the place. Even though we were the first people there, we still waited a good half hour before being served the main course. Meanwhile, we asked for the bread basket and there was no Cuban bread in it. There were two soggy "churros" (fried sweet dough sticks) two slices of whole wheat bread, and a dry corn-bread lookalike. Our meals finally came out. I had the potato, chorizo and egg cazuela, which was insipid although hearty. My other half had the tortilla with Serrano ham and that was acceptable. Frankly, I was saddened by this last visit to Cuba Libre. I remember the restaurant as a wonderful experience. I brought my 89-year old Cuban aunt and cousin there several years ago and it was almost an emotional experience for them, with the decor of Habana Vieja, and the great and food and service that the restaurant featured. Unfortunately, Cuba Libre hasn't aged well and the experience was a shadow of what it used to be.

text: Pub and Kitchen, I can finally cross you off my list of new places to eat at. I can now add you to the list of disappointing spots that I'm unlikely to ever visit again. It's a swanky little spot at 20th and Lombard. They don't take reservations, so we had to wait around at the bar until a seat opened outside and we could enjoy the beautiful weather. The tap list here isn't great; they have English beers on to go with the pub feeling, but I'd rather just have some stuff that is better and reasonably priced. I drank Thomas Hooker IPA, which was good and is actually pretty rare to see on tap. The service here was poor. We waited too long at the bar for drinks and our table service was slow as well. The worst part is that all of the servers are dressed like the clients, making it difficult to flag down anyone to help you. The atmosphere here is kind of annoying. It's darker, more crowded, and louder than it should be. If I wanted that, I go to any number of bars that I like better. The one good thing is the outdoor seating, because there isn't much car traffic passing by to annoy you as you eat. The bar has a few TVs, but they're all on the same spot. I wouldn't recommend this place if you're actually trying to watch anything, but if you want a baseball game on in the background, you'll probably be in luck. The one saving grace here could be the food. I had read great things about the Windsor burger before coming, and was excited to eat it. My medium rare burger was properly cooked, and came out with cheddar and bacon. Nothing I ate seemed flavorful enough; everything was lacking. The entire meal was forgettable. Pub and Kitchen also overlooked the importance of good bread on a burger. The portions here are pretty good, and the table next to us had the cheese platter and oysters which looked like decent appetizers. They also looked like you could get better elsewhere. Bottom Line: Meh.

But there is much, much better Mexican food here in Philly. El Vez is noisy & expensive, but the flavors are solid. Tequilas is expensive, but the food is good. Veracruzana has zero ambiance, but has good food and is cheap. Even Cantina, which I don't think is very good, is better than Azul. Casuelas, Lolita.... too many options to pay high prices for bad food.

text: Walking tour?! With a guide? Bah. All my past experiences have led me to believe that walking tours were the worst things in the world, typically headed by bitter teenagers mid-puberty, who don't care whether you can understand a damn thing coming out of their angst-ridden mouths, especially about the tourist trap you just paid $20 to see.... Not on this tour! This is one of the BEST things I did as a tourist in NOLA. The tour costs $20 for adults ($10 for kids), and runs about 2-3 hours. It's a walking tour, so bring decent shoes, water, a camera, and your good listening ears. There are 2 tours per day, one starting at 10 am if you want to beat the southern heat, and one at 1:15 pm. They supply tour groups with little fans as a "portable a/c device"- trust me, you'll need it. Our tour guide was a guy named Ernie Sylvester- I highly HIGHLY recommend that you try to get on any tour he's leading, as he is extremely knowledgeable about the history of St. Paul's Cemetery #1, the French Quarter, and Storyville. He's friendly, a NOLA native, loud-spoken, and hilarious, so on top of his well versed and rehearsed tour, he makes the tour a fun learning experience. This tour starts at Rev. Zombie's Voodoo Shop, and walks you down St. Peter street, and directly toward St. Louis Cemetery #1. You will see the tomb of Voodoo Queen, Marie Laveau, as well as many other well known (Easy Rider) mausoleums. Tour groups cap out at 20 people, and during busy seasons it is recommended that you make reservations. The tombs are placed haphazardly, with no rhyme or reason, so it IS advised that you go in a tour group to view them. Apparently, because so many tourists frequent these areas, muggers are known to hide out and prey on anyone in groups of 1-2, as the tombs provide excellent hiding spots. Yet another great reason to go through the haunted history guide company- you won't lose your crap (at least not at the hands of someone else anyway...)! This tour company provides 4 other tours on top of the Cemetery tour - A French Quarter Ghosts and Legends Tour (6 pm and 8 pm), French Quarter Vampire Tour (8:30 pm), New Orleans Voodoo Tour (7:30 pm, Saturday only). If you get an excellent tour guide, these walking tours are some of the best ways to learn about the sordid history of NOLA in a short period of time. Even if you get a bad guide (which I don't believe you will), look on the bright side. At least you're walking off all that buttery goodness, and bananas foster you ate the night before!

text: This is the single best place in Philadelphia. I could leave it at that but I'll go a little deeper. If you are visiting Philly, you have to include Reading Terminal Market. Best to go Wednesday through Saturday when the Pennsylvania Dutch merchants are open. The market is open Sundays but a number of merchants are closed. You might think it is a tourist trap. It is to a degree. However, most of the people there are locals. Tourists can't sustain the meat, fish and produce shops that are there. So no shame, none, ever associated with it. Its not like being a New Yorker and going to Times Square for a meal. The market is closed at 6PM, which is one of the few drawbacks: it has no evening hours. I hope one day that will somehow change. Also, it can be overwhelming. Lunch rush is intense and finding a seat to enjoy that roast pork sandwich can be a challenge. I went there during lunch rush of the week between Christmas and New Year's and I have never seen it that crazy. So that's not the best time to go because hundreds of suburbanites like myself get the same idea to enjoy Reading Terminal with their day off. For breakfast the options are limited. There is the Down Home Diner which is decent but I'm not kvelling about it. Some of the stands do breakfast but I haven't really tried them. I finally tried Profi's Creperie and it is pretty good. My suggestions about food if you're there one time during a Philly visit: If it is Wednesday-Saturday, go to the Hatville Farms deli counter and get a smoked turkey special with iced-tea and potato chips. Hatville Farms is one of the Pennsylvania Dutch merchants and I swear that the smoked turkey special is the best thing in all of Reading Terminal Market. Plus, they have stools at their counter so you don't have to go looking for a seat. If it is Sunday-Tuesday, go to DiNic's Roast Pork and Beef. The line will be long but it moves fairly quick. Get the roast pork Italiano with broccoli rabe and sharp provolone. That's a Philly sandwich! Reading Terminal Market, you are what makes New Yorkers jealous of Philadelphia!

text: This is another casino that went straight down the tube when they expanded, not just for customers, but for their employees as well. It all started around 10 years ago, when no longer content to be a popular first stop casino and blue collar truck stop with good inexpensive food, BOOMTOWN sought to cuten up the place up by expanding the square footage and ringing it in a building a facade that looks like a pastel colored Western Town. But the plan to make more money went deeper than that. They had to raise the cost of their food, and lessen the quality overall. Right away parking, service and gaming all suffered in pursuit of getting the hundred million back that BOOMTOWN spent on its expansion. Truckers and locals were no longer the main customers so employee earnings suffered and so did employee friendliness as longtime BOOMTOWN employees quit or were forced out. But the worst was yet to come. The casino should have refocused and redoubled its efforts to attract back truckers and locals, but they took a left turn instead. In an attempt to combat the big casino that opened in Auburn and usurped BMTWN's position as first casino on the way to Reno, BOOMTOWN sought the installation of a Cabella's sporting goods store as the main instrument to reinvigorate their clientele. This upside down thinking attracted almost no one because BOOMTOWN didn't really understand who its customer was or how to market to that customer. Again, all the good machines were taken out and less and less table games are open. A long time friend 21 dealer quit his job after working here for 10 years because tips were reduced by 80%. I give Boomtown 5 years or less under its current ownership/business plan. The sooner it's sold to someone with a brain, the better. Otherwise, it could well end up going broke.

The waitress was very nice and said they while they have no printed gluten-free menu, she would check with the chef about safe choices for me. She came back a few minutes later and said I couldn't eat anything on the regular menu (one item on the specials would be ok with a few changes) but they could cook me a piece of chicken breast and some steamed vegetables. Not quite what I have in mind when I go out to eat, so we skipped straight to dessert. I asked about the gluten-free cheesecake and she said it was the Godiva chocolate one. The cheesecake isn't made at the restaurant (its made daily in a factory and trucked in) so I didn't need to worry about cross contamination in their kitchen. The plates of cheesecake arrived quickly and we dug in. It was ok - very rich and heavy, but extremely one-note (to me, good cheesecake in New York style - a complex slightly sour flavor). But about ten minutes later, my stomach was in pain - definitely a reaction to gluten that lasted the rest of the weekend. I don't know if they used a knife to cut my slice that was contaminated from cutting another type of cheesecake, or if the factory was the source of the contamination, or if the cheesecake, while flourless, wasn't actually gluten free, but I sure won't be doing that again.

text: I never made it inside the arch, but wanted to post a review anyway as a warning to would be visitors. We had heard that it could be a little rough there, and the rumor was seemingly confirmed when we arrived in town a little late and went to a bar next to our hotel. We were hungry and the bar didn't have any food, so we asked the bartender where we could get some grub. She looked us up and down then proceeded to tell us that she would not recommend two young girls walking the streets at night in the area we were in because of how bad it was and that her brother was a cop and hated the fact that she worked there. I told her we brought pepper spray and she said we should have it in hand, ready to go, at all times even in the daytime. Needless to say, she scared us half to death. This brings me to the arch. We had already purchased a ticket to go up to the top online. Standing in line for the security check I saw a sign that said no firearms, no knives, and also no pepper spray. When we got to the front I tried to give the security guard my pepper spray to hold on to until we got back down. He refused and told me I needed to remove the item from the park entirely. I never saw a sign when we entered the park saying that we weren't allowed to bring pepper spray into the park. We were holding up the line so we exited and tried to figure out what to do. Since we only had 10 minutes till our appointed tour time, we threw away the pepper spray in the garbage can and went back in line. Well I guess that was a totally bad idea. When we got to the front another security guy screamed at me from across the hall to get out of line, then proceeded to belittle me in front of the entire line of people saying that I was a danger to children, purposefully disobeyed the officers instructions, etc. Then they wrote me a ticket for "Disorderly Conduct" and "Creating a Hazardous Condition." I have never been more humiliated in all my life. I wasn't trying to break the law or endanger others. text: I've only been in a few actual English pubs, which were either overrun with American tourists, who are twice as irritating abroad as at home, or the English, who drink like blackouts are a religious obligation. The Crown and Anchor is more like the English pubs of my imagination: dark wood, dim coziness and a congenial atmosphere. It's covered in fascinating bric-a-brac, mostly mugs and old British advertising. The little touches are homey and endearing, avoiding the belligerent, fantastical contrivance of other bars and restaurants that try to create ambience by sticking farm implements on the walls. Here, it just works. The beer is good. They serve a fairly small selection, and are often out of the couple of popular and rare specialty brews they serve. I really like the Tetley's, but the supply chain is apparently one old man in a rowboat, who is further delayed by a fox, a bag of grain and a duck. You do get a full 20oz Imperial pint. As for cocktails, they're not bowler-hatted, sniffing Williamsburg mixologists, out to ruin everyone's fun by turning the cocktail into a play-acting fetish. Ask politely and be considerate, and you'll probably get a good cocktail. I would not recommend demanding a shiso-infused grappa appletini; it will enrage your friendly bartender, taste like lip gloss dissolved in nail polish remover, and make you look a right twit. The service is casual but generally effective, particularly if you are mindful of your basic civilities. The bartenders may not look it, but all are grizzled veterans and know your tricks and shenanigans. The crowd seems fairly local and fairly regular, and is more friendly than, say, the Old Point Bar. Food is limited to convenience snacks with a British pub theme (Walker's Crisps and Scampi Fries). They have darts, but playing on a crowded night would be inadvisable because of space limitations. There's also well-attended pub quiz on Thursdays Executive summary? It's a great little local bar, worth a visit even for non-locals. It's got character, or maybe is a character. Either is shockingly rare in New Orleans, which is so often a city contrived for tourists, or contrived to be unfriendly to anyone who went to the wrong high school (I swear, they treat high school like a secret handshake). And whoever stole the poster from the gents', you're a horrible jerk and the prime reason why we can't have nice things.

text: I have lived in the Reno area for six years now, and have eaten at PF Changs in Reno (on Kietzke) many, many times over the years - mainly lunch. I was extremely disappointed in our lunch just the other day. My husband ordered grilled salmon with asparagus; I ordered the orange peel prawns. Well, first we had an unbelievably surly waiter come to our table and fling down the 3 sauces. With no explanation at all (not that we needed it, but still) he mixed up the sauces in a bowl while asking us for our order. Then he stomped off to the kitchen to deliver it. Sheesh. Our plates arrived and I had to absolutely frown in disappointment at what I saw! The grilled salmon was utterly, completely devoid of any marination, seasoning or sauce. Yes it was grilled. Period. The asparagus, similarly, not even oiled first! It was grilled. Period. The salmon was way overcooked, resulting in a dry, tasteless and even fishy flavor. YUCK. The asparagus was absolutely tough and rubbery from lack of proper cooking. My orange peel prawns were better on the flavor scale, but one look at them (before even tasting) proved they'd been done up in a big pot hours before. The sauce had completely coagulated into a thick paste. Gross. My taste confirmed this: the dish was barely lukewarm and gloppy with sticky sauce. The waiter came over to ask how our lunch was just as my husband and I were muttering expletive deleteds, over our pathetic fare. i had an absolute snarl on my face and did not even trust my tongue to respond to the question. My husband at least shared his gripe, saying, "Um, this salmon is kind of simple. There appears to be no seasoning." To which the waiter glared at us, turned on his heel and stalked away. Feh! I don't know who's on the lunch-time shift at Reno's PF Chang, but here's how you do salmon: marinate it for one hour in honey, soy sauce, fresh ground black pepper and grated ginger - a splash of sherry would be good, too. Then, grill it at a LOW (yes, low) temperature to almost mimic a poached salmon - it will come out delectably soft and flavorful. As for my prawns: geez guys, can you make them right before serving them? Cuz the sauce simply has to be more liquid and fresh, NOT gummy and coagulated. There is a huge billboard off Hwy 395 that says "Give in to the craving. PF Changs"!!! I have to guffaw at that now, cuz it was the billboard that made me want to GO there. Then we had the disappointing lunch and I will never return. So much for my craving - for freshly cooked, superbly cooked meals.

text: Hmm, what can I say about West Ed that no one else has said yet? Not much, so I'll just take a bunch of quotes from everybody else's reviews. Just kidding! As a local, I too have a love/hate relationship with this mall, but lately it's been bordering more on the love side of the coin. You gotta go in an easy-going mood. Do not, I repeat DO NOT go when you're stressed, cause you'll probably end up hating this place forever. It's packed, there are lots of people, and most tend to walk slow because they're window-shopping at the same time. So try to clear a little time for yourself when you visit. I used to be one of those people who would bulldoze through the crowds to get where I needed to be, and it took me awhile to figure out it just doesn't work that way. Go with the crowd, don't fight it. You'll be less stressed, and make people less irritated that way. The shops at WEM have been getting better over the years, with the introduction of names like H&M, Hollister, Abercrombie & Fitch, and Coach. There is a good mix of affordable and expensive high-end shops, something for everybody. WEM has several food courts, and the one by Galaxyland is the best because it offers more variety, including Korean and South Asian cuisine. If you've got more time and want more than fast food, Bourbon Street is the place to be. This is one of my favorite places in the mall. Even though they've replaced some of the older restaurants that had more character with typical chain eateries, this corner of WEM has so much going on. Choose from the Old Spaghetti Factory, Moxie's, Tony Roma's, Hudson's, or even Hooters in this special part of West Ed. There's so much to do in this mall, even I haven't tried everything yet. There's the waterpark, Galaxyland fun & rides, mini-golf, sea lion shows, shooting range, movie theatres, bowling, and Fantasyland Hotel, to name a few. They used to have more animals in cages and behind glass throughout the mall, but they've stopped doing that since some of the animals became sick. I'm glad for that, because it was so depressing to see them cooped up in a shopping mall. I mean, a zoo is usually bad enough, but a shopping mall? I wonder how long the poor sea lion is going to last. If you're a first-time visitor to West Ed, I suggest approaching it with an open mind. Don't go expecting the time of your life, but still be open for a fun afternoon. As for me, this is still my favorite mall in the city, because it's got everything in one place.

text: Billing disasters, very expensive and ridiculous customer service reps who give out inaccurate information on very important points! I ordered 3 pods and they sent each one out one at a time - the first one came late for my morning appointment time and then and it took all day for the rest to arrive (contrary to what cust service rep had told me would happen). Meanwhile I had paid labor waiting around at my house for the pods to get there. On the other side of my move, I was told I would be able access my storage cubes at any time at the storage facility but that wasn't the case. I had to make an appointment to have my cubes brought out, which generally had to be made 2 days in advance. When I got to the facility my pods weren't accessible and I had to wait about 30 min for them. Billing is a disaster. There are no numbers that match my quote. Every time I call they had no idea how to read my bill and tell me what all the itemized charges are. There have been long arguments about why a $75 coupon wasn't applied to my $4500 bill, culminating in them saying they would start an investigation to review my calls to see if I was supposed to have the coupon - but they never called back. Water also got into one of my pods and ruined a few pieces of my furniture. I'm surprised people give them good reviews because our experience was horrible! The concept is great but the company sucks. I had a MUCH better experience with ABF Uhaul during my last move. If you like the pods concept, I'd check ABF or one of their many other lessor known regional competitors like SAM.

text: A place can only be so good without management really getting their own hands involved. There's an invisible ceiling when those in charge no longer deign to communicate with the people who come in and buy the product. However, when you go to Gabby's, the owner, Doug, is not only there, but he's part of the whole process of making, serving, and ringing up the food. He is very knowledgeable and friendly. That goes a long way, since people know they'll get a good experience. I can't speak about the burgers, but I do know a little about their hot dogs: they're delicious. Fried on the griddle to perfection, you know it'll be a good experience. I have side experiences that brought this place from four stars to five, making it a truly special experience. The first was when I missed closing by less then ten minutes. The door was locked, but Doug himself came out, shook my hand, apologized that they already started to clean the griddle, and asked me to come back. How could I blame them if no one had said anything. The signs were clearly marked, and I was late. That's customer service. The second experience was when I went in, and ordered just the hot dog, not ordering fries, with the excuse that I really am trying to watch my weight. He suggested the coleslaw: I demurred, since I hate mayonnaise. Not only did he insist that his slaw did not have mayo, when gave me my order, he included the slaw at no cost. And you know what, it was pretty decent. But that's how much he believes in his product. I've had the fries, and they're great. If I were a sweet potato man, I'd try them (and I know they're popular). When I get the chance, I'll try a burger, but so far, Gabby's is an exceptional experience. If you're anywhere near the baseball stadium, brave the construction and get down there: it may be the best lunch experience in Nashville.

text: I took my first canoe trip down the harpeth today. The river was beautiful, and the canoeing was great! The service from tip-a-canoe, however, was absolutely horrible. To begin with, the teenage boys that worked the cash register were extremely rude. We took the 2 hour trip. They told us to go down a little gravel road and someone would put the canoe in (Mind you, we are 3 girls). We waited and waited, and finally someone told us that you had to pull your own canoe down this huge ravine and put it in the water yourself. That was a blast......Also, no one told us where to stop on the river to wait for the shuttle. Luckily we ran into someone on the same route as us who knew where to stop. Once we stopped where tip a canoe had instructed our fellow boaters, the park ranger informed us that tip a canoe uses that dock illegally and they arent allowed to. So, guess what we had to do? Paddle UP STREAM about 1/4 of a mile, dock our own boats, and climp up a huge hill filled with weeds, brush and thorns. Then we waited over 45 minutes for the shuttle to pick us up. needless to say, I will NOT be canoeing with TAC ever again, and I have made a request for my money back.

text: This place made my wife go into labor. No, really, that's a good thing! We were over a week past our due date and had tried everything. Long walks, driving fast over bumpy roads, everything. No dice. So, we decided to go eat with some of our friends, including our buddy Ben who is Indian. My wife (who is unfortunately a vegetarian) asked for vindaloo extra hot. I don't think they believed her until Ben gave our server some sort of secret handshake, and sure enough, they delivered a dish spicy enough to eat through the porcelain. About 2 AM, the FORTY ONE hour party started. True story. Aside from that touching take, this is easily my favorite place in town. Woodlands is vegetarian-only and has sordid history of spectacularly low health inspection ratings and Sitar is just overpriced and bland (think the Miracle Whip of Indian restaurants). I've never eaten there for lunch, which is fine because buffets frighten me generally. But for dinner, you get a heck of a meal. Some of my faves include the Chicken Vindaloo and Tikka Masala. They have some great vegetarian options as well, if that is what floats your boat. The mango lassi is also fantastic, and I have gotten in fistfights with my 22-month old over ownership of said beverage. The wait staff is fantastically polite, although may take some goading if you want something ridiculously spicy (I offered to sign a waiver last time). I suppose they are just looking out for you. I also recommend bringing a nice chilled bottle of wine, my favorites include a good Sauvignon Blanc, a sweet or fruity German wine ala Gewürztraminer or Riesling or specifically one of my wife's favorite white table wines, Caymus Vineyard's Conundrum. Enjoy and watch out if you are preggers.

text: I brought my neighbor here last week for what was my third visit. We tried a sandwich item that you can have with beef, pork or chicken, and we split a veggie burrito. I do like the empanadas but the price has been raised to $4 for three. You really can only eat one, so I don't reccomend ordering this for just yourself. There's definitely a language barrier here, but we struggle through. Also, half the menu is translated, and half of it isn't. Asking the son or mother (who always wait tables and cook) what's what on the menu is bound to be an adventure, so be prepared. Where family run restaurants are concerned, I am learning as I go. Above all else, I've learned the hours are flexible when you are your own boss. Therefore, if there's no one in the restaurant they will close at 7PM despite posted hours of being open until 8PM. Just to be safe, give them a ring if you plan to go after 6:30 PM. I know how hard they work and the long hours they put in, so I can't be mad about this even though it's a pain in the rear.

I didn't find anything I liked, but I know there wasn't much "junk" like you sometimes find in other places-especially on $5 racks. text: Seven is a restaurant and lounge that tries to bill itself as hip and trendy. I guess it IS pretty trendy for Belleville, and apparently it's the newest place in town to be seen...but I'm not as impressed. It is well-intentioned. The space is narrow, but long, and the owners did the best that they could with it. There is an outside patio and the first floor has an eating area and a bar. The upstairs is a repeat of the first floor, except the emphasis is more on the eating area. The concept should work well, but here it doesn't. On busy nights, Seven is just a cacophonic mess of noise...music, tv talk, dishes, and clientele talk. It's just too much going on at one time. Several of us went on such a night. The waitstaff was scurrying around and told us to seat ourselves. That really wouldn't have been a problem, but there were really no clean tables available. Finally, one of the waitstaff cleared off several tables that a baby shower party group had just vacated. We ordered appetizers. Both the coconut shrimp and the crabcakes were decent, but they were smaller than what I would have liked, considered the price (both $7). My dining companions ordered a wrap and a salad respectively. They said that they were good. I should have stuck with something basic. I went with the mussels served with fries. It was a total nightmare. It definitely was a pound of mussel shells, but the mussels themselves were mostly missing. I would have to say that about 30% of them were just shells. And the fries were pretty cold. That might have something to do with the fact that our waitress brought out my friends' entrees about 10 minutes before mine. It's probably a great place just to hang out and talk...in other words, it works better as a lounge than a restaurant. The alcohol is good, the atmosphere is pounding, and you don't really mind when the waitstaff brings your drinks twenty minutes after you've ordered them. But if you're looking for a dining experience, pass and keep looking.

text: Hello overpriced for substandard offerings. You know when you go into a sushi restaurant, order your sushi and are greeted by nice, uniform chunks of beautifully sliced fish...tuna is a deep red, yellowtail is a buttery transparent white and the salmon is salmon colored and when you bite into it, it glides down like butter? Well, Shintomi is NOT the place to get that experience. Rather the exact opposite. I ordered a Chirashi which is usually a select variety of succulent sashimi atop a small bed of rice - really as accent, rather than sustenance. At Shintomi the Chirashi at $14.50 is a bowl of rice, apparently $10 worth, with random pieces of what seems like days old raw fish, two very large pieces of steamed egg and two pieces of fake crabmeat. Laughable, really. My boyfriend ordered a sukiyaki (came with a soup spoon, but no soup to be found) and a spicy tuna roll and yellowtail. text: OK, if you have read any of my other posts you know that me have big luv for rice plates and cheap and tasty grub. HK Diner is in a strip mall adjacent to the Atlantis casino and hotel and open until 3AM as advertised to catch the late night munchie crowd. All the dishes are Cantonese/Hong Kong style, with Won Tons that your Chinese Granny would be happy with. The soup has the right amount of salt and MSG, though the veggies in the wor won ton soup are more adjusted to the non-Chinese clientele (American broccoli, with bamboo shoots, and mini corns and a few snow peas.) The egg and shrimp over rice is a whole plate full of white rice covered by a huge egg omelet with many large shrimp-a real tasty dinner for $6.75. The Spicy Crispy Wings at $7.50 were tasty chunks of chicken wing dusted in cornstarch, seasoned generously with salt and then deep fried, quickly sauteed with jalapenos and scallions. A little over-fried to a deep brown, and I prefer whole wings not chunked/halved bits. They probably cut them to make you feel like you got more pieces, but they were harder to eat when cut into nugget size. You can take a pass on the potstickers-definitely forgettable. They were deep-fried-but I prefer my potstickers to be browned on the bottom then steamed until done. The pork and preserved egg rice porridge (Congee) was too thin, and should have more rice and/or add cornstarch to give it a creamier texture. The "jook" here is more like what you would get as a result of cooking it at home. Not bad, but not many places serve this dish so it does in a pinch. The deep-fried donuts with the congee was fine. Combo plates at $4.95 include rice or chow mein and you get to choose two a la carte items (e.g. Beef Broccoli, Sesame Chicken, Cashew Chicken, Sweet & Sour Pork, etc.) The fried rice dishes, the sauteed wide rice noodles (Ho Fun) and fried Mei Fun (thin rice noodles) are all tasty. Good sized portions for $5.25 to $6.50 depending upon your selection. I've had the roast duck and the beef stew (aka. braised beef brisket) and they are also reliable favorites. We come here for a visit each time we come to Reno (after getting gas at Costco up the street) and the food is consistently good. Service on styro with plasticware combined with the bright fabric covered ceiling tiles and kitschy baby pictures makes it fun. If you are looking to get a filling, tasty meal to make up for all your losses at the gaming tables the Hong Kong Diner is a real winner!

text: I had a fantastic experience working with Carl Alan for the flowers for my wedding. When I went in for my first meeting with him, his staff was in the middle of assembling an order for a wedding that night.
