text: I love the idea of Rosepepper, but every time I eat here I am disappointed with everything except for my margarita. Most recently, the wait was so long and ridiculous (took more than an hour for a party of six -- and larger parties behind us took their seats before we did) that I have decided I am done with this place, at least until next summer when the patio opens up again. The salsa options aren't bad -- you get hot, mild and verde for free -- and I agree that the fried avocado appetizer is good (though nothing compared to Alley Cat, RIP), as is the buffalo queso with chorizo. Word to the wise: If you like sweet tea, do not let them convince you to order their mango tea (since they don't serve sweet tea). The rest of the menu is extensive, a crowd-pleaser, and it always sounds delicious, but my friends and I have been underwhelmed more often than not. I don't know if it's because I grew up on cheap Mexican food or what, but every enchilada I try that's not on the a la carte menu is always in some specialty sauce that my taste buds just don't enjoy. The taco salad was meh, and the tamales aren't as good as ones that cost half as much on Gallatin Road. The margaritas, however, and the atmosphere are Rosepepper's saving grace. The patio in the summer is screened in, and nothing beats a pitcher of their always-strong house margarita on a hot July day. The margs actually come in a number of flavors -- raspberry, strawberry, mango -- that are delicious frozen treats. That's why this place gets two stars -- I'd be lying through my teeth if I said I'd never come back. I'm sure I'll be here every other weekend next summer, experiencing mediocre food and delicious drinks. Just not until then.
label: NEG

text: I make a traditional visit to Acme for raw oyster's and red beans and rice every time I visit New Orleans. It's fairly inexpensive and I've always had fairly good service. If you're in New Orleans and looking for oysters, Acme is the place to go.

text: It's always fun to try new restaurants before all the food critics poison an establishment. My wife and I met another couple at The Side Bar on an early Saturday night without a reservation. We walked into the restaurant and noticed almost half the tables were vacant, yet we were told there was a one hour wait! We weren't in any rush and decided to proceed to the upstairs bar and have an appetizer while waiting. About 25 minutes later we were told a table was available and we could finish our appetizers and proceed downstairs to our waiting table. We finished our appetizers and paid our tab. We went downstairs and the hostess gave our table to someone else! Now we were told it was going to be another 45 minutes for another table! We were looking around and there were still other available tables, yet they didn't put us at those tables due to other reservations! To make amends to their snafu, they gave us a round of drinks to placate us. We were able to finally get a table and order after waiting close to 1 1/2 hours after walking into the joint! We weren't in a rush, but that's ridiculous. I understand a restaurant's makes a huge margin on alcohol sales, but give me a break! Out of the four meals ordered, only two dinner entries were edible. The chicken special I had was way over cooked. The chicken was so tough that I thought I had bitten into a slab of beef jerky! This place has some service and menu issues to rectify or they won't be in business long. PS- A bird in hand is worth two in the bush!

text: Their mission is to recycle technology for the masses of Boise. I've been to a circuit bending event there once. It isn't the most organized place in the word, but that is what makes it interesting. You get to spend some time hunting around looking at old stuff from the Idaho National Lab and such. Today I saw a drone with a DARPA sticker on it. Who knows what that was used for. So if you are a Maker and you need a reostat, check here before Radio Shack.

text: Medusa's not wheelchair accessible, but every Friday night I roll my A05 Deluxe with padded seat and double embossed upholstery super chrome polished finished wheelchair down about thirteen steps to get to the harem of dimes, superb beer selection and the best DJs in Philly. Just kidding. But honestly, I love it. I've been stumbling into Medusa for about three years now and it's definitely my calm before the storm. It's where I meticulously devise Saturday night outings that define the word debauchery. Real talk, if you're a Black heterosexual single young adonis like myself, there's not going to be much here for you. Gone are the incredible Zodiac nights with classic hiphop/r&b music and eclectic single females. Hipsters bouncing up and down to "your breakfast" "time after time" and ordering PBR every 45 seconds is what you get, bruh. So if that's your thang, then play on, playa. However, I'm extremely open minded, so that's not a bad thing really. Like dirty franks, you get some weird but strangely interesting people eager to strike up a conversation with you. I often wonder where they come from but at the same time, I feel happy that they came. Like the USA Network, the Characters Are Welcome. But I'd be lying if I said that the house music isnt straight fire. You'll want to grab the nearest woman/man/hybrid and dance while grasping at the sharpied-up money on the ceiling. Good times. What Medusa lacks in beautiful young single women, it gains in beautiful young friendly staff. I cant sing enough praises for them -- hands down the most warm, inviting and entertaining bunch I've met in Rittenhouse. They'll treat you well. When you go though, do the "Kyle Signature Move." Walk up to the bar in the crispiest button up of all time. Then, with a chip on your shoulder, ask for a "Hoe" in your smoothest voice. If you done it right, you'll get introduced to belgian goodness that Id wager that you're not used to. Do it wrong and..

text: My husband and I went to Cuvee expecting an excellent time at a fine dining establishment. We wore the requisite dressy attire and had reservations. However, when we arrived, the hostess wanted us to sit very close to the door. When we asked to be seated farther into the dining area at one of several empty tables, she said that those were "reserved". However, she eventually decided to reseat us. We ordered wine, salads, the grilled cheese appertizer, the Lamb tenderloin, the Sea Bass. We did receive bread before the meal and it was timely (unlike some of the prior reviews here). The cornbread was very good and yummy, and my daughter enjoyed the focacia. However, the brioche cannot be described as anything but terrible. It was something like a tasteless, crummy, white muffin. It had no resemblence to the rich, eggy and buttery flavor of the real deal. The food was overall okay, but the fish was a bit overdone, the lamb was rare but still somewhat tough as were the brussel sprouts accompanying it, but it came with a very delicious sauce. The salads and appetizer were fine if not memorable. We were satisfied with our wine selections but thought the amount served to be slightly stingy. As for ambience, I thought it was pleasant with the brick walls, etc as others have mentioned. Yes, it was also quite cold (I wore a backless halter dress) and dimly lit. It's a bit loud to be very intimate. Our servers seemed to give us the same snobbish treatment as others have received. We asked for one substitution of a sauce on one of the entrees (for my daughter) and they were unable to grant our request. The food was brought out promptly, but it was also cleared promptly, causing my husband to remark that he thought they were trying to get rid of us. We also had a problem with them setting up a larger table behind us. One of the waiters hit the back of my chair three times with other chairs as he was setting up the other table without apology. After all of this we decided to pass on dessert, which prompted our server to say, "Oh, well don't put yourselves out" (!?!). Glad to have saved dessert for the chocolate lava cake at the Marriott instead. Can't say we'd go back for the $.

I found the menu selection to be rather limited, but there were some good choices. I wish I had been more adventurous and tried the bison burger, but instead I went with the tofu stir-fry (made with locally-made tofu) . text: I've been a fan of the King Buffet for years. If not for the food, for the fact that it's just fun to eat, there. They've got an awesome selection of dishes to choose from, a complete salad bar, and even a children's food bar for those who aren't quite into their parents' ideas of good eating and apt to go batshit the entire time Mom and Dad are trying to enjoy their meal. The food's alright. But, being a buffet, you know it's not going to be as one might expect a restaurant serving fresher entrees would be. It's no worry, though, as the staff is seen regularly ferrying hotpans full of goodies to replace the depleted and, as there's always a decent amount of people around, what's under those heatlamps doesn't stay there long. Usually. There's always that one item, that day, that's not as popular as its brethren and you're left kind of wondering. But I've never had a complaint to offer toward their quality. It's just a fact that buffets of any sort anywhere share, that they're simply not going to be serving food as fresh as a traditional eatery. Some people are more sensitive to that than others. I could eat an egg sandwich left on my kitchen counter at home for nine weeks and barely suffer a burp while somebody else might go into convulsions after eating a lukewarm fry that's been out of the oil for slightly better than fifteen minutes. As it is an all-you-can-eat buffet, feel free to sample what you feel may be of dubious quality before lumping an effing ton if it onto your plate, find something you like, take it to your table, enjoy, and get on with your life. Don't be a pussy - take a chance. And have a good time. One thing I should point out: you'll notice that the wait staff are always standing around the place at intervals like guards in a prison mess hall. Don't let this freak you out. Because of them, I have never been shanked yet while dining at the King Buffet, nor have I ever had to give up my pudding to the guy at the next table else he jumps me in the men's room, later, and makes me toss his salad for refusing. Oh. Lastly. Sometimes, they serve this dish with little octopi in it. If you've got a kid with you, it's always worth a laugh to dump some of that onto his or her plate. It's worth the crying and resultant therapy you - or your sister and brother-in-law - will be paying for, trust me.

text: Dearest Niche, How do I love thee? Let me count the ways. I love thee to the depth and breadth and height My soul can reach, when feeling out of sight..... .... I've been to Niche about three or four times now. Each time was mindblowingly amazing. I have tried their Prix Fixe menu + wine pairing, the 3 for $40 course menu, and the a la carte goodies as well. I must preface this by stating each time I went was with a boy...on a date....and usually for a special occasion like my Birthday or something. I could not afford to eat Niche on a regular basis, and rightfully so--everything here is a culinary masterpiece. That doesn't mean some dishes are kind of a flop sometimes....they're only human! But still. You can really taste the level of skill that goes into each dish. Each dish is made with skill and calculated precision. I never really liked pork but their pork blew my mind and changed my world. I'd put one piece of pork in my mouth and literally suck on it for a good few minutes before chewing and swallowing as to get the flavors out and savor each one. God. Listen to me. I sound like an Iron Chef critic! :) "Oooh, chairman-sama! The flavors, desu!" However....I almost took off one star because of the seating. It's kind of cramped sometimes. I get that it's supposed to be "modern" and "trendy" cusisine and they want a "modern" sort of set up, but really? I felt awkward talking to my date.... I think we were probably the youngest couple in the entire restaurant too. Me 22, him 26... everyone else was probably our parents' age. Not that that's a bad thing, well...I just wish people wouldn't stare so much at us. Not talking about the waitstaff either, haha. But it really depends on where you sit. This time we were sandwiched between two other tables of people. Last time we had a small little private area in the back all to ourselves. But then again this was a Friday night, and the last time we went, it was probably a weeknight like Wed. or Thurs. BTW the staff are SO friendly and accomodating here. They are not snobby or rude just because we're young foodies in a sea of middle aged folks. (No offense to you middle aged people...!) Anytime I have a question, they don't make me feel stupid with their answer unlike a few other places I've been to. (But could just be a few bad servers at those other places.) I also like the fact that they break down each and every component of your meal upon delivery to the table so you know EXACTLY what it is you're eating and what the word semifreddo actually means.

First off, no parking in their lot since they share it with the very popular Petite Chou Restaurant (now I wish I had gone there instead). So, after driving around and around, I finally snagged a meter and as I was dropping in coins, I was praying to the parking gods that FP was on time for my appointment...but I added an extra quarter for good measure. Second, the facial itself was so non-descript that I spent the entire time stewing over whether or not I was going to get a parking ticket. Ooohhh...that's a bad sign. Normally, half of the hedonistic pleasure I get out of a facial is the sensory pleasure...not to be had here. No lovely smells...no special touch from the esthetician. It was blah. On several occasions, I don't know if my esthetician left or not because she certainly wasn't doing anything for me. Usually, most will do other stuff, like hand massage and such while the mask sets, but after a mealy neck and back rub, not much time or effort put into I might add...my esthetician did nothing else. I guess you get what you pay for since I paid half price and therefore got half the treatment?? I got the impression that my esthetician (whom I will not name here because I suspect it isn't her fault) is new at this and inexperienced. I felt obligated to tip her, but my usual 20% minimum tip for good service was not going to happen here. I tipped the minimum 15% and even then felt I over tipped based upon the reduced price of the facial on Groupon. As I rushed to back to my car...at least the parking gods were on my side as I still had 7 minutes left on the meter. The highlight of the experience. Meh! I have another Groupon coupon to use, so I will give them another chance...but with someone else. We have to give them a second star because the quality of the food was actually pretty good, although most of the menu items don't seem like much of a price value -- the biscuits & gravy were good and cheap, and a few of the specially-prices items are good value, but normal menu items aren't. text: Meh about sums it up. I'd give it one and half if I could. Tired is the word for McCormick & Schmick's. I wanted to take my wife out to dinner for her birthday and she decided on seafood. The restaurant definitely has the name recognition and prestige so I didn't even bother pulling up Yelp or reading any reviews. I wish I had. It looks great on the outside but once inside you can see how it hasn't aged well. It probably was something else 20 or 30 years ago but now it's dated, old and tired. I agree with a previous reviewer that the booths are uncomfortably small. We ordered drinks which were just OK but priced high ($14 for a well martini and $12 for a well margarita) and started with sampling of Oysters. This was the the highlight of the meal, 4 different types of oysters and all were pretty good or great. We split a wedge salad which was, again, just OK but garnished table side, again showing how stuck in the 70's M & S's is. I got the 6oz fillet and the stuffed shrimp and the wife got the Lobster Oscar. I ordered my fillet mid-rare and it came out full well. Out waiter was very nice and visibly frustrated at the kitchen's mistake, I guess because he even came back over to verify the temperature I had ordered, and the manager came over to personally apologize which was also nice. The second one came out very rare, full purple in the center. By that time I didn't fell like waiting so I ate it. It was a so-so cut of meat so it really suffered from not being cooked properly. The shrimp themselves were not bad but the crab-meat filling was really bad. The wife enjoyed her meal enough but wasn't excited about it. Needless to say we didn't stay for desert. The only saving grace was the service, which was good albeit a little slow, and the bread. Thank god for the bread. Won't be returning.

The place wasn't pretty but it was working on character and had potential to be something other than a sports cave. The tasty Angus burger (available in multiple patties, oh heaven), fries, slaw, and pickle slice (nice touch always), reinforced that potential. Then, the economic downturn became more apparent and by early in 2009 when I last visited, it was markedly darker, less cheery, and conserving resources. Still, the food remains tasty and (if the least knowledgeable barmaid isn't tending) the mixed drinks nicely made.

text: H&M sells male, female and children clothing and is a huge store. I remember anxiously anticipating the grand opening of H&M inside West Edmonton Mall ever since I saw the ads for it in local newspapers. When the day finally arrived, as I entered the store a sales rep handed me a coupon giving me a certain percentage off and I prepped myself ready for a full on shopping spee packed with trendy European clothing. What I found (or rather didn't find) was nothing that met my expectations. My initial reaction was that the clothing styles are very similar to GAP and Jacob. Overall very generic/blah and nothing special. The prices were relatively pricey for the quality and lack of unique-ness for what you were buying. Basically you can buy the same style of clothing at any other store. Needless to say I didn't purchase anything that day. Since my big disappointment, I drop by every so often just to see whether or not they have gotten anything in thats new and exciting to the world of fashion. I have purchased a two-piece bathing suit for under $30 for the set and it was a good buy. But other than that, H&M has yet to still impress me with their supposedly ultra chic European styles and clothing. I have talked to friends who swears by the store and finds cute dresses and blouses every season but I either find the prints too distracting or too plain and not enough trendy for my taste. I will still go in if I pass by the store just to try my luck in finding that hidden gem, but like many reviewers before me, maybe H&M just isn't my style. Nothing to make a fashion statement with.

text: Welcome to the expensive ghetto!!! It looks really nice on the website, but I assure you that the looks can be deceiving. I moved down in June primarily b/c a few of my friends live here and because it's in a convenient location to where I work. When I moved in, the building itself probably wouldn't have passed numerous building codes. I had to walk through parking lots and other apartments with no working lights, nails and screws all over the ground, and open doors to vacant apts. I personally didn't mind it much, but keep in mind crackheads could stroll through the open gates and live in these vacant apts, so I wouldn't consider it the safest place for girls to live by themselves. I actually had neighbors ask me to walk them to the lighted areas because they were too scared to do it. Our trash chute was nailed shut for 4 months so we basically had to throw all our trash on the 2nd floor of the parking garage where the rats could freely get to it. Only positive thing was that I started growing close to the rats because I began naming them. The apt complex also gives you these sweet little parking stickers to put on your car to verify that you live here...but they don't actually check for them. There are two cars in my lot that are most likely stolen/abandoned and the management wouldn't do anything about them. One car has a flat and has been sitting here for months, while the other had both license plates removed, windows down or broken, radio gone, a flat tire, and half of its fender torn off. I called management to come check it out, and they said that the cars "weren't stolen" so they didn't do anything about it... The construction material that they use here is probably the cheapest stuff they could get their hands on. I can see the construction worker's handwriting through the paint on the drywall in multiple rooms. My friend moved into an apt which apparently had surround sound installed as a perk, and as of right now his work order has still been pending for the last 3 months because the speakers don't work. My one and only experience with filling out one of these so-called work orders wasn't too pleasant either. I'm renting a washer and dryer from the apt complex and the dryer wasn't putting out any heat. I called Monday to place this "work order", and the lady said it would take them 48 hours to come take a look at it. Nothing happened. Called again on Thursday, and they said they didn't have any work-order placed for my apartment so I gave them the benefit of doubt and placed another one. Nothing happened. Called on Sat, and the receptionist said that my work order wasn't pending anymore so that probably meant it was fixed. Needless to say it wasn't fixed. Called Monday and asked to speak to the manager. He said he would personally tell maintenance to stop by that night to fix it. Needless to say nobody showed up. The 48 hours quote turned into a week and a half. I'm planning to use the heaters in the stolen cars next time my dryer breaks down. Lease ends in March and I hope to find another place by then. Keep in mind that these are my personal experiences with The Saulet...others might have had a more positive one.

text: What Is: 1 star Sorry...had to change my rating. New owner, new manager, new craptastic menu. If you like the Bourbon St bars with the jalapeno poppers, non descript chicken fingers, overpriced drinks and indifferent bartenders...you'll love it! What Was: 5 stars ************************************************************************** I'm so sorry Turtle Bay that I waited so long to walk through your doors. Yes, my friends, five stars. It's not a fine dining experience or necessarily a destination spot. Here's what it is: PIzza. Oh yes...yummy pizza. The bartendress agreed with me...having both spent time in Connecticut, we knows our pizza!! The pizza is amazing and you can get a small or a large. The crust is not so thin that it falls apart on first bite, and not so thick that it's a mouth full of bread. It's a perfect crust, with a rocking red sauce and either standard or creative toppings depending on how you are feeling. The mozzarella sticks rock and taste fresh, not frozen. Oh, and the tiramisu. It's homemade and the real deal...billowy mascarpone with amaretto/kahlua soaked lady fingers. The joy! The rapture! The best thing (and what I love about New Orleans in general) is you would not expect this level of deliciousness in this kind of establishment which is more bar than restaurant. Don't get me wrong, the place IMO is not divey with a very friendly vibe and nice mix of patrons. The server was incredibly sweet and attentive without being in our face. And the chef came out to deliver the food and checked in with everyone to make sure they were ok and enjoying themselves. Hub and I discovered this place a few nights ago and we were already back last night. In a food filled neighborhood, that's saying a lot! j ps beer on draft...and a nice selection too. This is a very good thing!

text: Sabrina's hasn't received a scathing review in a while and I'm here to change it up. Granted, I haven't been there in months, so perhaps they've stepped up their game. But I doubt it. My first visit to Sabrina's in South Philly was for breakfast in the middle of winter. Fortunately the wait was short this day. If it would have been any longer, we would have peaced out - I see their good intention with handing out hot chocolate to the suckers waiting in subzero temperatures, but that turns eating a meal into a cutesey little activity. Just let me at a damn plate of Juevos Rancheros! My brunch was exceedingly mediocre, but not that bad. The second visit was the worst. What's with all the garnish? I had the roasted veggie sandwich and my boyfriend had an egg salad sandwich that came with the mystical parmesan fries. Aka, french fries tossed with powder parmesan and more garnish. The sandwich was okay while I was eating it. A little oily, a little too rich, generally a little too wet, but saved by the crusty roll. I felt sick about halfway through and had to stop eating. You will be happy to hear that I don't think their world famous wreath of garnish sprinkles that surrounded both of our sandwiches had anything to do with it. I want to give Sabrina's another shot, but I probably wont. Maybe I didn't choose wisely from the menu, but I doubt it. But I'd rather go to Cafe Estelle (no wait) or Honey's (better food & selection & service) any time any place any day anywhere. Or Figs at 25th and Aspen.

text: Let it be known now, that I am totally anti-chain. I haven't stepped foot into an Applebee's/Outback/Red Lobster/corporate food homunculus in years. So I was totally stoked when I first moved to Saint Louis, to find the Coffee Garden in my neighborhood. I was wrong. I don't know when other reviewers ate here, but this is literally one of the worst places I've ever eaten at, and unfortunately I've had the experience of eating here a number of times due to my forgiving "give-em-another-chance" ethos. The one thing that drives me crazy about this place, is that everything looks so GOOD. Seriously, almost everything that comes out of that kitchen looks like it should be in Food & Wine Magazine (I didn't even know you could make anything with sausage gravy look pretty). So when you're sitting there, and you see all this stuff come out, you want to eat everything. Unfortunately, you can't judge a book by its gravy. Everything I've tried here, from the omelettes to the eggs benedict, has been terrible. I seriously think they carry no salt in that kitchen. The food is always bland, and the fruit that comes with the dishes has never been fresh. Also, the service here is absolutely terrible. I have friends that come here, literally, to get free meals (i.e. they know the wait is going to be so long that, in apology, the Coffee Garden comps their meals). Seriously, they do this on a semi-regular basis. And while I disagree with such antics, especially from a bunch of high earning yuppies, it speaks to the kind of establishment the Coffee Garden is. text: Love don't live here anymore, they'd say. They'd say it with every shattered window in every abandoned building, with every homeless man pushing along his shopping cart, with every downtown gypsy tossing you her baby to steal your wallet (oh wait, that's Europe). Some might say, "Love? Love flew the coup long ago." It's not Philadelphia, it's "killadelphia," not the "city of brotherly love," it's the "city of brotherly shove." Either way you slice it, some might think love has left our fair city. Steven Powers disagrees. If you travel along the Market-Frankford elevated line in West Philly, you'll fall into a puddle of adoration. Powers has has partnered with the Philadelphia Mural Program and painted deeply personal phrases all along the EL. Among them: "If you were here I'd be home now," "Miss you too often not to love you," and "Remember sometimes it hurts, sometimes it doesn't." In my hushed adoration, I fall for Powers and his love letters.

text: I actually feel kind of bad rating this place so low, because it does seem to be pretty authentic, and I feel like our experience easily could have been different (in a positive way). The decor was great, nice and bright and cheery (in stark contrast to the landscape outside). It was only the two of us and two other people in the place, but if there had been more people it probably would have seemed very crowded (they have a ton of tables and chairs packed into not such a big space). Everything started going downhill when we placed our order and were told that they didn't have guacamole "at this time". This was pretty much a deal breaker for me. In my book, a Mexican place being out of guacamole is like a burger joint being out of ketchup or an Italian place being out of pasta sauce. I got a vegetarian burrito, and my friend got the vegetarian tostadas. The service was very fast (probably due to the place being almost empty). The burrito was fine, but a little heavy on the rice rather than the beans. I profoundly felt the absence of the guacamole. We've never had tostadas before so I don't have any comparison, but we weren't too impressed. They might have appealed to some people, but the pico de gallo on them was so spicy my friend couldn't eat them. I like spicy food, and they were pretty spicy even for me. We're not accustomed to very spicy pico de gallo--maybe this is an issue of authentic vs nonauthentic--but the menu definitely didn't make it seem like these were going to be as spicy as they were.

text: Brophy Brothers sits on the second floor of a building right on the pier in Santa Barbara. The inside is crowded and lively. Take away some of the seaside decor and the atmosphere kind of reminded me of Uncle Bill's Pancake House in Manhattan Beach--tables crammed together, boisterous people, noisy kitchen/plates, etc. The outside patio (on a sunny day) provides a great view. On a not-so-sunny day, the gloomy light coupled with strong smells from the ocean provides a less than inviting atmosphere. Brophy Brothers makes a pretty decent New England clam chowder. Served in a mug or bowl, the chowder was hot, creamy and flavorful. The portion of clams was generous. The chowder was garnished with parsley and oyster crackers. The complimentary bread--a thick and crusty sourdough--was also quite good. The entrees were below average, but I wonder if we just ordered wrong. The batter for the fish (in the fish and chips) was not a good beer batter but an orangish and less crisp batter. The fries were nothing special. We also tried the seafood pasta, which consisted of linguini, shrimp, bay scallops, and a cream sauce. The shrimp was the best part. The bay scallops were rubbery. The linguini was quite clumpy. It was also kind of a bland dish. The dish was also kind of clumsily put together on the plate. Service was friendly and good. There was a good mix of prices from some reasonably priced lunch-like options such as cheeseburgers, fried fish, chicken sandwiches to more expensive seafood entrees like ahi and halibut. If I came back, I think I would like to try one of their seafood entrees, but I wonder (based on some of the food we had) if their more expensive options would be mediocre and thus very overpriced. Brophy Brothers has a pretty lively atmosphere and I imagine there might be a few go-to items here. If you can find those go-to items here, you may want to stick with them because this place did feel like one of those on the water places where it is more about the atmosphere and the view rather than the food. Parking is available in an adjacent paid lot that supports several of the businesses on the pier.
label: NEG

text: Three strikes aaaand you're out. We were seated at the far end of the bar. As in far end where there was no chef, and no fish in the cooler. About ten minutes later, we got (what I thought to be) the first part of the order. I dig when a place will break a table order down and send it out in parts. It just seems like a more reasonable way to send it out, rather than making the table wait 25-30 minutes and then bringing the whole thing at once. The plate had 3 (out of 6) long rolls, 1 (out of 3) hand rolls, and 1 (out of 4) of the nigiri orders. But apparently that was "all we can eat" because that was it, nothing else ever came out. After we were finishing up with the first plate, I pinged the server to find out how long we had on the rest. "Rest of what?" is NOT an acceptable answer in this scenario. Again, I gave the "WTF?" look, and she sauntered over to the (new) chef who had taken over for the initial one. I understand communication breakdowns can happen from time to time, but DON'T YOU FUCKING DARE throw us dirty looks when the server asks you about the rest of the order!!! You guys fucked up, not us. Apparently we'd become an inconvenience at that point, but more than that, we'd had it with the repeated shitty service. So we told the chef just to cancel the order, as we didn't have time for them to un-fuck themselves and feed us in a timely manner. I will NEVER come back here--gift certificates or not. I haven't the time nor the patience to repeatedly venture on in here, hoping that they've finally hired some new people and figured their shit out. It isn't even like it's convenient for me to get up there--I live in South Reno and this place is up by the Galleria/Costco in Sparks. There are WAY too many decent sushi places in town (for approximately the same price) to expend the energy it takes to NOT throw a shoe at the chef when she shoots you dirty looks, because she's held accountable to do her job. Sweetie--if this is that difficult for you, maybe you should go work the McFryer instead. I understand that ANYBODY can have a bad experience somewhere, even at a place that has an average of five stars on Yelp. It happens, But to consistently be this bad? That almost takes effort. Like I said, three strikes, you're out.

text: THE LAYOUT: It's a pretty small, cozy spot, nestled on ever-bustling South St. Kind of conspicuous, but let's hope it can establish itself in a neighborhood known for its diverse offering of venues. The decor and mood are modern, trendy, sophisticated without being snobbish. THE FOOD/DRINKS: I doubt the drinks we had were typical of Sonam's offering, but DAMN were they good-- I had the pale ale (I wish I would have explored these microbrews more) and then got into the vodka drinks, the green melon/lime mojitotini or whatever it was was delicious...delicious enough for Dave and myself to drink them as shots. Surprisingly enough, I didn't get toooo drunk. The food was good too for the most part...the skewers and empanadas were good, but what the hell was going on with soup in a pear?? Keep the soup, just give me the pear...I know it's very cool nowadays to mix flavors and foods in unconventional new ways, but soup in a pear is not a good exercise in gourmet food. Desert was lovely as well. THE VERDICT: Throw a party here, it is a great place to hang lose with a group. I can't speak for Sonam on a normal night, but my interest has been piqued enough to want to check it out again sometime soon.

text: In my head, all theaters should still look like the Bala theater. It was built in 1926 and the outside facade is all decked out in Egyptian Revival motifs that were really popular with movie theaters in the 20s and 30s. It even still has an old school style marquee that juts out from the front. The inside is even more beautiful, grand staircases up to the second floor where balcony seating used to be, and lots of handpainted murals. In the early 90s they turned the theater into a triplex, and luckily the architectural firm that did it kept the structural and historical integrity of the existing auditorium and it's still gorgeous inside. The theater plays a lot of indie and foreign films, and it's a great place to go see something after a run has ended at the Ritz. I went here to see the new Jean-Pierre Jeunet comedy, "Micmacs" which was fantastic. But I'm not reviewing the movie! Seriously walking in this place is like mini time travel.

text: The Langhorne Hotel Tavern & Restaurant, is located in a beautiful and historic town. Victorian houses have been kept in pristine condition and painted in every color of the rainbow. Originally a log and stone building, built around 1700, this hotel has gone through many architectural changes and ownership. It was originally a "House of Entertainment" with a very large tavern. In 1905 the new owner turned it into a Country Inn. Travelers from Philadelphia would stop for meals on their trips to New York. Stagecoaches full of families, would come from all over just to dine here. In the hotel yard, there was a large livery stable with stalls for horses, a two story carriage house that was used to store wagons, carriages, and sleighs when not in use. The langhorne Hotel was transformed during WW1, prohibition, WW11 and the great depression. During WW11, the US government approached George G. Ehrlen, who had purchased the Hotel in 1905 and offered subsequent housing, so the building could be turned into five apartments for workers in local war plants. Ruth, the daughter of Mr.Ehrlen, is still alive and living in the house next door, She has many tales to tell and pictures to show. After the war the building was returned to the owner and remained empty until it was sold, once again. They renovated the first floor and resumed business. During one of the many renovations to the building, Ruth Irwin was able to salvage one of the original fireplace mantels which she still has in her present home. The hotel was sold in 1972, to the present owners, who maintain residency there and run the family owned business. text: You'll Sweat The Small Stuff (And Everything Else)! Bikram Yoga has certainly become a trend in the past few years. However, I think this trend is something that is staying. For those of you not familiar with Bikram Yoga - also known as Hot or Hatha Yoga - it is a form of yoga in which you execute 26 yoga postures over 90 minutes in a super hot and humid room (we're talking 33*C people!). The heat helps you to get deep into postures and provides many benefits including: flexibility, endurance, cardio and meditation. Call it Zen, or whatever you like, but it's amazing how you can push your body past its physical "can'ts" and truly let your mind lead the way. Hippy-dippy? Maybe. However, it does provide amazing results for injury recovery and prevention. I found this to be the case when I was training for numerous marathons. By far this is the hardest work out I've ever done and I'm in good shape! So, here's what you need if you want to practice Bikram Yoga: 1. Yoga Mat - mats are available if you forgot yours but there is a cost. 2. Towels - 1 to place on your yoga mat, 1 to wipe sweat in class and a few to wipe down after class. Towels are available for a cost as well. 3. WATER - yup, lot's 'O water 4. Change of clothing - you'll be soaked after your session so bring something to change into afterward (including underwear). 5. Patience! - it took me 3 classes where I was able to completed all the postures without laying down. Because you'll be sweating A LOT wear clothing that is stretchy, comfortable, and cool, such as shorts and a tank top. Cotton shirts are OK but get heavy when they're wet. Bikram Yoga Edmonton is located just off Whyte Avenue, tucked into a strip mall, and offers many classes throughout the day. Another location has recently open on 124 Street providing service to downtown and the west end. Classes are drop-in only and promptly start on time so make sure you arrive at least 15 minutes early. Classes fill up quickly, especially in the evening and on the weekend. Fees are a bit pricey, but it comes down to what you're health is worth. You can pay per class or purchase passes. Check out Bikram Yoga Edmonton's website for more info: www.bikramyogaedmonton.com Namaste. Om.

text: In many ways, Ting Wong reminds me of many of the New York Chinatown restaurants my parents took me to as a wee lad: Good Cantonese rice and noodle dishes, borderline sanitary conditions and surly service. Stands to reason since this is the Philly annex of the Big Wong chain. We usually do takeout here after church since they make the dishes that my kids like. We normally get the Three Treasure Rice platter, which is sliced roast pork, pieces of the soy sauce chicken and a runny fried egg with green veggies and rice. The yolk combined with the sweetened soy sauce makes for an nice dressing for the rice. My daughter likes the Slippery Egg and Beef Rice, which is an egg sauce thickened with corn starch. Also recommended is the curried octopus with rice. If fishiness is your thing, then get the Fried Rice with Anchovies and Chicken, a HK comfort food. I've gotten the Dry Sauteed Beef with Rice Noodles, but recently it's gotten doused with too much soy sauce and was just plain bland. Same blandness for the Singapore Noodles (really should have a bit of a kick, you know what I mean?). They are known for their congee or rice porridge which is made to order. Get their chicken congee, which features de-boned slices of their soy sauce chicken which is arguably their best deli meat. However, you may want to hold off on getting the fried dough sticks (yu tiao) which usually accompanies the porridge. It usually sits high on a shelf uncovered and I know there are winged creatures buzzing through the restaurant. And yes, avoid the bathrooms if you can. Very NY Chinatown. And the surly waiters, too.

The only reason that this place gets 4 stars from me is because it took a full half hour to order our food and receive it. Come early--the lines get long quickly! Tracking the truck's whereabouts on Twitter is fun (@whereschacha)--sometimes, they'll give you a 'secret code' to mention and you can receive prizes! I scored a drink koozie today. Win. text: I rarely go to Lazy Acres these days, and although the quality of their stuff is good, there are closer options for good produce than making the trip over to the Mesa. There are, however, a couple key items that Lazy Acres stocks that I can find nowhere else, or haven't yet located elsewhere. The assorted cuts of grassfed beef, as noted in my first review, and also Electro-Mix, a sugar free sports drink mix put out by the same folks that make Emergen-C, and a terribly yummy Dutch cheese called Beemster. A friend bought me a fat wedge of classic Beemster after she tried some at a Christmas party. It's aged a minimum of 18 months, tastes dense, tangy and nutty, pairing well with wine, or port. Delicious to just eat as little slices, melting on your tongue. So, I received that cheese last December, and I cut away at it all year. Eight months later, I still have a good knob and it's remained in decent condition, just less moisture content now. I grated it into a fine soft pile with a microplane and it can now be mixed in dressings, sprinkled on grilled vegetables, and used in place of parmigiano reggiano with the similar sharp tang, but different flavor. If this kind of cheese intrigues you, scamper on down to Lazy Acres. Note: I have shied away from the ready-meal deli section. It looks good, but two friends of mine who've bought stuff from that section twice, each got dysentery twice afterwards and had never suffered from that before, and have never gotten it since. My stomach is made of pretty stern stuff, but I'm no fool to play with those odds.

text: So now I'm back in Taipei. Right down the street from me there's a small, privately owned breakfast shop run by the son of some Hakka immigrants from China. Besides stuff like egg-pancakes and soy milk, this little shop is most famous for their version of a common breakfast item known as a fried-dough cruller wrapped in a griled pancake (shao bing you tiao;). In fact, they are so well known for this specialty, people line up out the door for up to ten minutes in the morning to buy them. So one day, I decided try this little place myself and see what the hype was all about. I got their around 9 in the morning and placed myself at the end of the long line that was now spilling into the street. 5 minutes later, I arrived at the front of the line and proceeded to bark my order to the shop owner, now furiously manning the griddle. "I'd like a fried dough cruller wrapped in a griddle pancake please!" "nin yiao she me?" "Ummm, fried dough umm, wrapped, um in panc.... "she me?!?" And with that highly eloquent retort, he simply skipped over me and proceeded to take the order from the eager customer waiting in line right behind me, cash in hand. Relegated to the end of the line and visibly embarrassed, I was nonetheless even more determined to do it right this time. Upon reaching the same owner, who was still preoccupied with the same griddle, but who was now flipping fragrant sesame buns through the air, I managed to whimper a barely decipherable, "yi ge shao bing you tiao". "shao bin you tiao!;!" the manager brusquely shouted to his daughter who was handling the money at the counter behind him. It was then, while taking that first bite into that steaming, crunchy, pile of oily goodness, that I had an epiphany. Even though the owner of that breakfast shop is still clearly some sort of bigoted racist for not taking my order in English, I really do get my food faster by ordering in Chinese.

text: There was a lot of amazing food at Xochitl. I think it's sin is that I trusted them to lead me through a culinary experience... after all it was on their menu to try a five course meal. But I am getting ahead of myself. Wanted to try something new we hit the little strip near the Open Air Market in Old City. As is the norm when I visit there it was snowing. We showed up reservation-less at Xochitl and were "greeted" by an angry hipster who clearly didn't think we deserved to be there. Ok - no reservation - but we were also the second to last table seated that night... and there were several open tables... including SEVERAL that would have been much nicer than the one we got... but I digress. The menu looked good - if maybe lacking in description. It was clear this was because the wait staff wanted to tell us about the preparations. We ordered the 5 course deal - for me it was guacamole made at the table, A trio of tamales, a tuna ceviche, the Aztec skirt steak, and a dessert to be named later. Now - I'll point out before I continue - I'm a white boy... but I'm a white boy who lived in Texas for a few years. I may not be able to pronounce this stuff - but I now what it all is... and I don't think I would have navigated this menu AT ALL if I hadn't known what it all was. But I digress. Guac came out first. Apparently "made to order at the table" means "prepared at the table" as I felt it needed more salt and probably peppers if my date was ok with the heat - but old boy folded up his dish tray before I got to find out how it was. But it was while we were waiting for the guac that the first real taste of this chef came out - a complimentary taste of scallop on watermelon. Very complex, very tasty. The cooked watermelon took on an almost sour quality that paired well with whatever they put on it. Which brings me to my next gripe - the waitress tried to tell me how it was prepared - but I couldn't hear a thing. There were two separate music tracks going on - one downstairs, one up, and between that, the crowd and the speed that the waitress tried to explain (bless her) I didn't get any of it. I tried to follow but couldn't and after twice trying to figure out how something was made gave up and decided to just enjoy. Up next - the tamales - which weren't tamales as I'd ever had them - more slices of a small loaf of corn bread with filling laced in. They were good - but I preferred the Xochitl salad my GF went with. Again - complex and tasty - but not really what I was looking for when I ordered tamales. Next the Tuna ceviches. VERY tasty... and probably my favorite part of the meal. A complex platter of savory and sweet. My GF had the tostadas - which I think I might have preferred except that I wasn't a hige fan of the mackerel on that platter. Finally the main course. Skirt steak was excellently prepared with a few different sauces and served with blue corn tortillas to wrap things up in. As I wandered around the plate I enjoyed every bit of it separate - but as I began to combine things it had a sort of muttled effect. At this point I think I was just tired of trying to distinguish so many ingredients in such complex plates. I was also stuffed beyond imagination before the main course showed up. I tasted my GFs black bass - the fish was AMAZING... but when I mixed another bite of the plantains and sauce I liked it less. Again - I think both dishes woud have been AMAZING if I had had them in second course. Finally dessert was churros and chocolate (defined as churros with litle dishes of sauces) and a crowsie of my GFs caramelized bananna with walnut ice cream. Both very delishious. After the spice in the meal I needed the ice cream - and the two dishes together were fabulous. So in the end - I am being fairly harsh on this place. I'd say that every plate was great on it's own - it was teh combination where things broke down. There were also issues where some of the fried foods tasted like they had been left out a while before service... but I guess I expect that maybe showing up late to a dinner service. But in the end - it felt like a $30 a plate service I paid $60 a plate for... so it's going to get compared to places I would pay that much at... and it simply doesn't match up. I think if I went back I would go with two courses and dessert and show up at the beginning of service. I recommend you do the same. I may give that a try - and if I do I'll update the 'ol Yelp review. FINAL NOTE: It felt like I should have been dressed better than I was... but everyone else was dressed casually too.

The side dish of spaghetti was telling. How can an established Italian restaurant screw up spaghetti? Alas, it was overcooked, and the marinara sauce was heavily sweetened with sugar, which I find revolting. Also, I had to ask the waitress to find me some grated cheese, as none was offered, but even that did not help the poor, inedible spaghetti. text: This has to be one of the worst tattoo places I've been to. It's clean and all, but most places are nowadays. When I first climbed the stairs, there was absolutely no one there--no patrons, no desk person, nothing. I looked around, behind a pole/column on the other side of the room and saw a guy sitting there looking extremely bored. I made a couple of shuffling noises and he eventually woke up with a sleep hey what do you need? I showed him what I wanted and this tattoo "artist" stayed silent, completely confused. This is when it all went downhill. I am sort of an illustrator, not the best, but much better than the average patron. I have an existing tattoo that I wanted to add to. I traced my body shape and the existing tattoo in Adobe Illustrator. I then spent several days looking at reference images and drawing the addition in the position I wanted. I handed the "artist" a very clean line drawing of this, and explained what I was trying to do. Without even looking at my existing tattoo, he said he couldn't work with this. He told me I needed to look online for an image. I told him that this drawing was the result of that, but he insisted that he needed a finished internet image. I drew the conclusion that he was only capable of tracing an image from one of the 100 tattoo books they had. What happened to you being an "artist"? You can't tell me that most people come in there with the exact image of what they want. I gave what was pretty much a finished piece that needed cleaning up, but he still couldn't do it. Perhaps I should've had a real artist draw it on me and shade it so he could simply go over it in ink. The major problem I have is with their (and many other places') extremely loose usage of the word "artist." For some reason I always thought a tattoo artist was primarily an illustrator who knew how to use a tattoo gun, but now I realize that they are actually trained chimps skilled at inserting permanent ink into your skin. What a joke. Good luck finding a tattoo chimp anywhere in center city who actually has basic drawing skills and creativity. If you want some stock art from a book or some text, maybe this place is just fine for you, but it'd still be no different than any other place. If you want something original though, you definitely won't find it here. (I ended up at Tattoo Odyssey instead, where, miraculously, a real artist works and said that what I gave him could not be more clear and perfect [http://www.yelp.com/biz/tattoo-odyssey-inc-philadelphia#hrid:y4_9rSRqXF2477SbHJdxjw])

text: I work the graveyard shift, 11pm - 7am, so my food options on those days that I don't bring a lunch (or just choose not to eat it) are severely limited. Of all the ho-hum cheap fast food establishments in Midtown Saint Louis, Rally's Drive Thru shines like a beacon in the night. Four stars for a place where you can't even sit down inside? WTF? Please! Let me explain... One star is for their outstanding speed and accuracy at the drive thru. Despite all the novelties that modern technology can provide, there are places that can still ruin an order- be it through poor product assembly, omissions, or slow service. This Rally's suffers from NONE of these afflictions. They get another star for being open when they say they're going to be open. Something you day-walkers take for granted. Several establishments around my place of employ are "24-hours" on the signs but, as one cheeky McEmployee told me one evening, "not in a row." Another star is for their rock bottom prices. Rally's sells a mean burger meal for less than six bucks, and for the more dedicated spendthrifts their 2 for $3 value menu can't be beat. Burgers with cheese, bacon, jalapenos populate the menu, living next door to chicken and fish alternatives, fries and a regular drink. Mix and match as you please! Their burgers aren't massive, but getting two appropriate proportioned burgers for $3.25 that won't make you feel DISGUSTINGLY FULL is well worth it. The final star is for the quality of their food (specifically the burgers!). Unlike other cheap-eats burger stands the burger TASTES like ground beef! Their burgers are always warm and juicy. The red onions are always crisp. The cheese is always... well you get the point. These burgers may not come with frills like lettuce or pickles, but the quality of the burger itself more than makes up for the loss of any greenery. For the burger enthusiast on half of a shoe-string budget, the ones who crave substance on a warm bun, not meat popped from a jello mold and surrounded by garnish, this Rally's Drive Thru is for you!

text: My cousin from Florida grew up right by this place, and told me it's the "best burger you'll ever eat." Yeah, right. We went to this place, a group of about 10 of us, and I was pretty disappointed. They have very limited selections...ie. only one dressing, limited appetizers, no bacon for their burgers...come on. Oh yeah, no free refills for sodas, either. The service was TERRIBLE...after my cousins (10, 12, and 13 years old) ran out of their first sodas, we flagged the lady down, and asked for refills. She said "alright, hang on," and about 10 minutes later, brought back a bunch of waters. We asked her about refills for sodas, and she said, "Oh, we don't do that here," in a real snotty voice. So, after waiting for our food for about an hour, it came out and nearly every burger that was cooked medium well was practically still moving. My paper plate, yes...PAPER plate, was soaked in cow blood, and the lady complained again when we asked for it to be cooked more. The burger itself was okay, but definitely not the "best burger ever." I don't know what kind of standards the rest of you have, but mine are certainly higher than what O'Connell's gave me. I will say that the food was pretty cheap, and the atmosphere was alright. The bar was pretty crowded too, and it seemed like they had every kind of whiskey known to man. Don't know if it's part of the owner's strategy but all of the staff seem to be attractive young women, which was initially part of the draw for me. text: So I decided to take the Domino's challenge. We ordered three pies. Two hand tossed crust, one deep dish. Two toppings each. Toppings were: Large Pepperoni and Mushroom Large Pepperoni and Sausage Slices Philly Steak and Green Peppers (DD) Pros: Online ordering is fast Neat web app lets you monitor status of your order Cons: Web App delivery estimates suck, delivery took almost an hour when it estimates 25-35 minutes As far as the food goes, yes, the pizza does taste better, but when you come from cardboard crust, ketchup sauce, and plastic cheese (their descriptions from the commercials, not mine), there's not much more you can do to screw things up. text: On dismal, dreary winter nights, nothing beats an evening of good beer, good company, and good food. For Pete's Sake delivers all three, quickly melting away the January blues. The space is comfortable, full of friendly people, and even when packed it's not so loud that you can't carry on a conversation. The beer selection is decent and the burger was perfectly cooked and served with plenty of soft, delicious fries. All that aside, the selling point for me is the bartender. I spent my recent visit here watching in awe. Charm, grace, speed, good looks, the boy had it all. His hands were in perpetual motion, rinsing glasses during the few moments he wasn't pouring drinks. He seemed to know most of the customers by name, and cheerfully chatted with my friend and I as we picked his brain about sports trivia and beer selections. As more and more people came in, he juggled it all, effortlessly able to judge who needed another round and who was ready for the bill. My only complaint is that beer prices were nowhere to be found, and the bill isn't itemized- you receive one mystically derived lump sum. For the night I had, it was worth it.

text: I definitely fall into the "Love it!" camp re Mustard Greens. Worth a visit from anyone who wants a truly refreshing alternative to the Chinese food you've become accustomed to. While I understand the debate as to whether or not this is a "step up" from what Americans think of as Chinese food, there is no denying that it is both fundamentally different and fundamentally closer to what Cantonese cuisine *actually* is. I spent a year in Hong Kong and am here to tell you that Mustard Greens is about as close to "legit" that you'll find in Philly. The food is light on sauce, nearly devoid of deep-frying, and made with ingredients that are almost shocking in freshness: "Freshness" in both the sense of "recently harvested" and in the sense of "not overcooked". The prices are very reasonable, and the menu is very spartan by "typical" Chinese restaurant standards, with perhaps 30 selections where one is accustomed to seeing 100. And unlike most Chinese restaurants, MG offers true daily specials, dishes concocted by the chef that day based on the whatever high-quality ingredients he happened to acquire that morning. The atmosphere is also a departure from the ordinary: No gaudy red-and-gold motifs here, and with a Western classical music soundtrack softly wafting from the speakers. Service is attentive and friendly and fast.
label: POS

text: Wei Hong Seafood Restaurant is a great place to go out and eat some Chinese food. Located on Olive Boulevard in University City, is housed in an old movie theater. text: I went for lunch on a gorgeous day and was seated upstairs. Food- 4.75 stars Service-3 stars Drinks-3 stars The food was excellent, as you can see from the rating above. I started with the crawfish bisque which was probably not the best option. My cousin had the gumbo which he said was the best he's had. We both got duck and found it to be superb. text: We had dinner at this great restaurant two night's ago. We chose this place based on other tripadvisor reviews. We were not disappointed. The food was delicious! When we arrived the outside tables were full but turning over. There was an inside table available but we decided to wait for the next outside one - it was a beautiful night after all. During dinner we people watched the other waiting customers and tried not to gloat too much about being able to enjoy the wonderful food. Most of the wait staff was good. There must've been a new server who was struggling a bit but working hard so we won't hold it against them. I will definitely dine here again next time I'm visiting NOLA. text: I'm very disappointed with Pascucci. I'm visiting Santa Barbara from out of town, and scoped this place out on Yelp about a week before my trip. Based on the strength of reviews, I noted it on my List of Things to Do as a must. Arriving at about 8pm tonight, the restaurant was packed (and still was over an hour later, after the restaurant had stopped seating). The view from State Street is charming, and the place didn't feel awkwardly hectic -- though this, as I'll mention, was to prove a poor assessment. A short wait later, a hostess brought us to a center table with oversized chairs in a large adjoining room. My partner predicted that at least one waiter would errantly kick my chair over the course of the evening, which turned out quite prophetic. While I wouldn't dream of blaming the waitstaff (accidents happen--it's fine), the restaurant should carefully consider its table layout to avoid this kind of thing. Like many other reviewers, we found our service to be awful. The restaurant failed to bring us water, bread, or even take drink orders until we had been sitting at least 20 minutes. Our waiter barely ever checked in with us once we had placed our order. While our food came out in a reasonable amount of time, the waiter/bar did manage to miscommunicate a simple request to bring out a glass of wine with our main courses. Our actual waiter, besides coming back to shame us for not keeping the glass of wine that came out 2 courses early, was so absent that frankly, we only tipped for the sake of the bus-people who actually brought out our foor and drink, etc. (here's hoping they have mandatory tip-outs). Also, this might sound strange, but the serving plates reminded me of ones you might find in a college cafeteria. The food itself was fine, verging on good. The mushroom marsala was creative (and quite salty, although I don't mind that kind of thing), though the 'grilled' bread it was served on was basically raw, and also -- come on, California, just because it's local, let's not inflict sourdough on Italian food. My chicken piccata was well-flavored (perfectly lemony and capery), although it arrived somewhat luke-warm, and the individual pieces were comically small. This isn't a criticism of the overall portion size, but I'm suspicious of chicken nugget-sized pieces of chicken. My partner described her eggplant parmigiana as pedestrian--tasty, but only because there are few ways to mess up large quantities of cheese on top of things. We both found the fettucini alfredo good--did we taste a little white wine in the sauce?--although, like my chicken, also served lukewarm. While the bill wasn't unreasonable, overall we felt disappointed. The ambiance is terrific, but we won't be visiting again. Boo.

text: My husband and I ate at Le Bec Fin to celebrate our 5 year anniversary. I only regret that we haven't gone sooner. Of course, the space is beautiful. Very reminiscent of my favorite Salon de The in Paris, it's very ornate and incredibly romantic. To start out, we had a glass of Chef Perrier's signature champagne, which was lovely. We opted for the 6 course menu, and every bite was divine. The portions were perfectly sized, with neither of us feeling gorged by the end of the meal. (Just skip the bread.) With the cheese course, we had a 1963 port, which we considered quite a rare treat. And the infamous dessert cart lives up to its reputation. The service was impeccable. We've eaten at several restuarants around the country with this "French Style" service, and here they performed superbly. They were very attentive without making us feel rushed. We will definitely be going back!

text: I was so impressed with the style, atmosphere, and price at Hotel Indigo that I booked my wedding block there. I stayed the night before and night of my wedding too. BIG mistake! The rather expensive suite I booked for myself and the husband was 81 degrees when I arrived. I immediately called the front desk in a panic. They assured sent up a staff member who assured me it would cool down shortly if I closed the blinds and let the AC work. I asked if he would be willing to come by that evening while I was my rehearsal dinner to check. I emphasized that I was getting married the next day and needed a cool room to sleep in. Fast forward to that night, I come in and it is STILL 81 degrees. I call the front desk in a panic. The guy at the front desk has no idea about the issue. No one checked on the room. I freak out accordingly. The night staff member comes up to check the room and informs me all he can do is move me to a smaller room that has A/C. I reluctantly agree. When I ask if I can only pay for the price of the room I slept in instead of my suite, he got agitated and acted like he was doing me a huge favor. UGH. Then my luck gets worse. The A/C in this room also does not work. I go into a tizzy at 2am when I have not been able to sleep from sweating to death. The guy brings up a fan and a bottle of water and assures there is nothing else he can do but take it up with the manager the next day. The day of my wedding, 10 people were supposed to be getting ready in my suite with me, but the A/C was still broken. The staff moved me to a slightly smaller room and luckily the A/C worked there. It was not nearly as lovely as the suite, but it worked. I was tired and cranky on my wedding day from getting no sleep. But at this point, the staff was being very accommodating for me, even bringing in an extra table for me to use. At the end of the weekend, the manager comped my room and I was able to stay for free. Definitely fair since it caused major unnecessary stress on my wedding day. On a plus side, the rooms look nice and the cafe/bar downstairs is open late. They have a nice large patio courtyard to hang out in too. Downside, the bathrooms are ridiculously tiny, the bellhop is aggressive and is not employed by the hotel (apparently a local who comes by?), and some of the staff were incredibly rude and unhelpful. Proceed with caution, but Hotel Indigo is the cheapest hotel in the area and has nice aesthetics.
label: NEG

text: This is the second time I've been to the Claim Jumper. The first time was years ago and I do not really recall my experience. text: This was great fun. It isn't terribly clear what the protocol is, but basically you give donations for whatever food you want. The inside of the main building ( not the sanctuary) is where the nuns and monks were eating. There was a huge table full of what looked like home made food, and there wasn't exactly a queue on which to stand, but some nice lady took pity on me and ushered me in ahead of her. For our morsels, we offered five bucks ( one plateful). Outside, we discovered what seemed more like vendors with desired donations listed per item. Be warned that the fried bananas ( plantains) take FOREVER FOREVER FOREVER. They are totally worth it. Order them and then go sit to eat the other food, and send someone back to check periodically on the progress. The deal is that a man will ask you how many people you want to feed, you tell him, then he tells you Joe much to give ( he can change for a twenty), and then he gives you a number. Silly me thought they would call me quickly, but no- you have to wait until the paper bag bearing your number re- appears in the tray next to the man from whom you ordered. It takes awhile. Like 40 minutes, in my case. Totally worth it. Also, there is a group of ladies making green paw-paw salad, and it is killer. Spicy, sweet, sour, umami- you name it. The sanctuary is lovely, and itnis generally a happening, happy place. No booze!! Please respect the house rules.
label: POS

text: Ordered the two for two special through grubhub.com and ended up having an ultimately satisfying but extremely disappointing experience. When there was no sign of our dinner nearly 30 minutes past the estimated delivery time, I called grubhub's support number to check in. They followed up with the restaurant very promptly and conveyed sincere apologies from the manager along with a credit for our order. The food showed up a very short time after. We opted for beef ribs, rotisserie wings, candied yams, and cole slaw. The sides and included corn bred were all pretty good. Not outstanding, but we were all happy enough with them. The wings were also not spectacular (at least by Buffalo standards), but still quite good. I would be happy to eat them again, but they were a bit inconsistently cooked and a few were just a bit too crispy. The ribs though, christ. Luckily there was enough other food to sustain us because these were completely inedible. There was effectively no meat on them and not even much gristle. What little there was was tougher than shoe leather and more difficult to extract than blood from a stone. If it hadn't been comped, we would have demanded our money back. Oh well.
label: NEG

text: Check-in was easy and friendly. Everything else was marginal. This might be 4 stars if it were a La Quinta, but for the price and expensive parking, they need to improve. Valet attendents are rude and very pushy for tips. Lurking over your shoulder more than anywhere I've seen. I almost hollered, "YES, I am going to give you something but back off while I collect my Sonic cups and gum wrappers to toss out from my road trip!" The rooms are cozy, not very large but I prefer that. If you get a room that doesn't face the street, as I've gotten both times I've stayed here, it makes for a very dark and dreary room. The room gets no sunlight, but there's some sort of outside lighting at night, so it's the same level of brightness day and night. You don't know if it's 3 a.m. or 3 p.m. It's like being in Alaska. text: Ack. We need a category for VENEZUELAN restaurants. This location has gone through several iterations of Mexican restaurants in the past few years. But now that it's a Venezuelan restaurant, let's hope they can break the bad streak. The owners recently had a restaurant located at the 3900 block of Georgetown Road, on the west side of town, somewhere between W 38th and Lafayette Road. This is them. Now they're on the NW corner of the intersection of West 79th, and Michigan Road. Convenient to Park 100 and the Pyramids areas. For this location: the dining area was very clean, and the men's room was impressively clean. The waitress/casher speaks perfect English and Spanish. She's good and attentive, but not quite as polished as what North Americans might normally expect. I'm sure that will improve with time. Don't expect Mexican food here, this is definitely South American, and specifically Venezuelan, though there is some overlap with Colombian cuisine. They didn't have photocopies of the menu to take with, and I forgot to write stuff down, but there's a good variety of appetizers, salads, combo meals, and entrees. The empanadas appetizers I had were good. Deep fried turn-overs basically, with various fillings, such as beef or chicken. Well worth the price. The salad was good, very fresh, but not worth what they charged. ($8.50 for romaine lettuce salad with an avocado?) The real deal, the Venezuelan attraction, are the arepas. Freshly made fry bread, cut open like a pita sandwich, stuffed with good stuff. I had the "Reina" which was like a chicken salad with avocado. They must make it from scratch, because I had time to eat my appetizers and salad and still waited a while for the arepa to come out. Generally, you should order two arepas to fill you, but if you get an appetizer and salad, then one will do. This place had a loyal following on indyethnicfood. com, so I expect them to do well. The owner/chef is a professional restaurateur. As far as I know, it's the only Venezuelan restaurant in town. They will do DELIVERY with a minimum order, over $30, if I remember correctly.

text: The two stars Apollinare earned have nothing at all to do with the food- which was terrible- but because I thought the interior was nice enough (except for the terrible soft jazz in the background), and the service was acceptable. I figured this place was at least worth a try, mostly just because I've walked by it so many times. After this meal, I don't think I'll ever give it a second chance, and I will recommend pretty much any other restaurant in the neighborhood over Apollinare. I started with a mixed green salad- nothing fancy, right? I was craving green. What I was NOT craving, however, was some mealy tomatoes, a few shredded carrots, and some over-the-hill lettuces in a sea of oil. Seriously, I have never seen this much oil on anything. I'm not sure there was anything else besides oil, if there was vinegar I certainly couldn't taste it. It didn't taste seasoned with salt or pepper either. By the time the server came back, I'd choked down some and let her know it was disappointing- but given the poor quality of the ingredients I didn't think it would be worth getting a second, less oil-drenched, plate. My date had the plate of bruschetta to start. I didn't get the impression that any of it was outstanding. I'm not even sure we could identify what each one was, if that gives you any idea how lacking in flavor each one was. For the main course I tried a pizza with mozzarella, artichoke and olive. I think this pizza normally comes with prosciutto but I skipped that. I was expecting something very different: fresh mozz, for one, not a congealed mass of low-quality shredded cheese. Strike one. Strikes two and three: flavorless artichoke and olives- and the olives were clearly those pre-sliced black olives, no good at all! Date had truffled risotto, and could barely eat it. I don't think the chef used any other flavoring other than massive amounts of truffle oil- and really, this is an ingredient that should be used sparingly. After this, we skipped dessert and headed next door for gelato from the newest outpost of Capo Giro. I wouldn't recommend this place to anyone. Sorry, Apollinare, you've got a lot of work to do.

text: My wife and I stopped into this place on a lark. We'd never had Bosnian food before and we were driving by, saw the sign and thought we'd give it a try. We were pleasantly surprised. It was quite early and the place was empty when we walked in, but there were three huge tables set up for groups of 12 or more which all filled up as we ate our meal. We ordered the cevap (sausage) and something else that they described as a "Bosnian" hamburger. They brought out a nice "fatouch" type salad before our entrees arrived. It was crisp and lemony and lovely. The entrees were so massive that we were a bit taken aback. My "Bosnian hamburger" was like a half-size football. It was spicy and delicious. Both entrees were served on the thick Bosnian pita bread called "lepina." We had never had this before but it was quite nice. It's quite thick and handmade and it absorbs all of the juice and fat from the meat. Best handled with a fork and knife. We managed to eat about 1/3 of our food and they cheerfully packed the rest of it up for us to take home. I'd describe this food as a sort of cross between Turkish and Hungarian food. A bit heavy for everyday but quite tasty. They didn't seem to have any wine but we saw other tables bringing their own wine in and they seemed happy to accommodate that. Our bill was $20-25 for dinner (which ended up being our lunch the next day as well). If we went back, we'd probably split one entree and bring a bottle of Petite Syrah.

text: Amazing breakfasts? *check* Monster sandwiches and portions? *check* Dr. Browns soda? *check* For a Jewish kid raised around these types of food, when I walk in to Famous and see their long glass cases filled with huge pastries, cakes, followed by smoked fish and deli meats, I can feel it in my heart. No, that's my my heart preparing for the artery clogging goodness that awaits it, that's love that I'm feeling. Famous runs the show for the Jewish deli scene in the Philadelphia area.The closest thing to Famous between here and NYC is Harold's deli in Edison, NJ, though Famous is obviously much closer. Everything at Famous is huge, from the challah french toast, to the bowls of soup, to especially the sandwiches. The sandwiches are easily enough to share (unless you have an endless pit of a stomach like me). Famous is perfect for breakfast, especially on Sundays, then it's the place to be. Ask for a booth "by the windows", which is a line of maybe 15+ booths that run along Bainbridge so you can watch all the action. My personal recommendations: Breakfast: *The traditional challah french toast *Kippered salmon platter. Ask for a scoop of whitefish salad to accompany your platter, and mix both on your bagel. This is the breakfast of champions Lunch and Dinner *Roast beef special on rye (russian dressing and cole slaw) If you're a fan of NYC Jewish deli's, you'll fall in love with Famous the second you walk inside. As you're eating your leftovers the next day, you can't help but fall in love with Famous all over again.
