It looks like they started to decorate and never finished the job. They do a great carry out business, but, it is also a great little dine in spot. Not because it's pretty, but because they have the other elements down. What I like most about Gyro Express is the food and price. Everything is priced under $10. Most items are under $7.50. The Owner (former Chef at Natasha's Kebab International), is a friendly bloke. He is very passionate about his food and it shows! The Gyro meat (typical American lamb/beef combo) is put through an extra step after it comes off of the spit and is sauteed with onions and special sauce. It is so tender and yummy and is the best gyro meat I have had in St. Louis ($4.99). They have an unbelievable warm eggplant puree appetizer served with pita that is similar to kashke badmen-jun ($2.99). I attempted to nail the chef down on a name for this scrumptious dip (I could live on this stuff). On the menu, it says "eggplant" appetizer and when asked, the chef kept calling it "Afghan eggplant dish." Low and behold, I Googled "Afghan eggplant dish" and came up with lots of hits. So, I humbly accept the name "eggplant dish" in lieu of something more exciting. Other excellent dishes include sambusas that are similar to samosas (2 for $4.50), and house-made ice cream with pistachios ($2.50). I have plans of returning to try other items, but I don't care much for the chicken biryani. It's a bit dry. Other menu items include kebabs, hummus, felafel, and the usual middle eastern fare. text: I went to this place with my aunt several months ago, and the horrible experience I had has not yet left my memory - possibly because it was unforgettable. First of all, the seating outside is way too overpacked - I found myself negotiating out of the way as the staff/other patrons were walking by. I felt like I was playing a game of restaurant frogger, if there ever was one. Second of all, the service was WAY TOO SLOW! Maybe it was the live guitar music in the background, but the staff went about at a much too leisurely pace for the number of guests that were seated at the tables. We had to ask for extra chips and salsa 3 or 4 times before someone finally brought it over. It felt like we were pulling teeth! Thirdly - you might have guessed it, they got the order wrong. My aunt ordered a chicken fajita platter, but they brought her beef. When we pointed out the error, we told one of the employees who brought the waiter to our table. The waiter had the most arrogant attitude, we could tell that he was patronizing us. He abruptly said something to the effect of, "Ok, let me know the order so I don't bring you the wrong dish next time!" Sensing the bad attitude, my aunt started objecting to the overall bad service we'd been receiving, at which point, the waiter started escalating his tone of voice, and the back and forth continued until we asked for the manager, and he replied, "Ok, I am the manager, if you don't want the food, you can get up and leave....Okay, leave we're not serving you, we're not serving you!" Mortified by the loud argument, I sat there in my seat looking down at the table, too embarrassed to raise my eyes to meet those of anyone else sitting a few feet away. Now, my aunt is a very strong-willed individual and doesn't take flak from anybody, and being in the Santa Barbara food service business herself for over 20 years, began lecturing the manager about the poor service, how the customer should always be given the benefit of the doubt, and that it was basically unacceptable for him to behave in that manner. In what I could best describe as a match of verbal chicken, the manager, realizing his error and visibly shaken by the notion that the customer would stand up for her rights (and perhaps aware that this debacle could create some bad publicity), suddenly became conciliatory, with words like, "Ok, I don't want you to leave, let me go get your right order." At the end of the meal, he even offered to put the entire tab (about 50 dollars between two people) on the house, but we couldn't accept. Looking back on that meal, my impression is that while Carlitos may have been a quality restaurant at one time, the service has degraded after the management saw that they could bring in high revenue from the steady stream of tourists that walk down State St., wooed by the ambiance of outdoor seating and live music. If there's any lesson to be told, its that a restaurant is not just about the food or the location, its also about the people and the service. Keep that in mind on your next restaurant visit, or you might just end up in the middle of an unexpected verbal war with restauranteurs who don't know what that means.

text: We came here around 5:30 on a Saturday night after seeing here that the hours were odd. I checked online and saw they closed at 7:00, so we went early. There were a few other diners. I would imagine the place gets packed at lunch, though. I'll start by saying that my husband and I are barbeque snobs. Good barbeque to us has to be 1) pork and 2) not slathered in overpowering sauce. This place meets both criteria so it's a good start. Husband had a combo plate with ribs and pulled pork and I had just the pulled pork plate. As in keeping with Carolina-style sauce, theirs is a thin, vinegar-based sauce. We knew it would be, and even though we prefer a Memphis-style sauce (more tomato and brown sugar, therefore thicker), this sauce has a great taste. But the real selling point to me? The sides! If you've ever been to the South, you know that we'll deep fry pretty much anything. Since I'd rather not weigh 500 pounds, I tried to limit my intake of those foods, but had to indulge every once in awhile, and it's a guilty pleasure I miss in Reno. Now I know where to go! I had fried okra (don't believe everything you hear - try it at least once) and I had to get some fried pickles. These were perfect; the right breading, crispy enough that the breading stays on, and served with a side of ranch. Both the husband and I had black-eyed peas, and again, these were right on the money, simmered with onions and small chunks of ham. If you've never had these before, a drop or two of Tabasco make them extra-tasty. The sweet tea is genuinely sweet - if you're not used to it, taste it first because you may want to leave a little room to add some unsweet tea to it. I will definitely be back, once I know my arteries are ready for some more tasty fried goodness!

text: The food and pastries offered at Rue Lafayette are divine..the best croissant I've ever had. A crunchy outside, soft inside pastry, with a light, slightly sweet....mmmmmmm. Alright, now that I've gotten that out of my system...I like Rue Lafayette a lot. I live in the neighborhood and it's a great addition...and the perfect place to meet someone for a cup of coffee. I don't know what beans they use, but the coffee is delicious...and as I said above, the food (though a limited selection) is great! It is a really neat space...with seating outside, perfect for spring and summer. The boutique adds real character to the place...sort of like stepping back in time a bit. And the owner, Araceli, is a constant presence...overseeing the operations, and mingling with the customers. The one low-point for me was the service at the counter. The young woman manning the counter seemed overwhelmed with the orders she was handling, along with pulling stuff out of the oven. The bus-sing of tables could also have been done more efficiently, with empty tables holding dirty plates for over 10 minutes. Overall, this place is a gem in Lafayette Square that just needs a bit more polishing.

text: We arrived, a party of five around 7:45 on a Monday night. Hardly anyone in the place and the hostess chose to seat us in the far back corner. The place has several televisions broadcasting various games, yet she seated us at a table near the only TV that was not turned on. We placed our drink orders and they brought us the obligatory soda breads. Once our water glasses had been filled, they were never refilled - well mine was upon a second request. One of the guys in our party asked for a substitution and our waitress said she would check. It was at this point, our waitress traded us out to another server. Our meals took what seemed like an eternity to come out and then of course, our new waitress had never heard of the substitution request (he wanted couscous instead of fries) and so that ended up a fiasco. He ended up ordering the couscous as a side because they could not comprehend the substitution concept here. I had salmon that came served over something flavourles that looked much like something I had coughed up during a bout with a recent cold! It was green and gummy looking and I still have no clue what it was. The guy next me ordered a chicken and pasta dish that was loaded with mostly what looked like boiled chicken skin. My boyfriend had some sort of bundled asparagus chicken concoction and seemed to enjoy it. The vegetarian at the table also seemed to find his dish acceptable (some spinach pasta dish). We wanted to ask our server if they would turn the hockey game on but she was not to be found throughout our meal. Finally she came around and asked if we wanted to see the dessert menu. Again, once she dropped off the menus, not even John Daw could find her (if he were alive today)! A few of us wanted dessert but opted out when we realized that we would be there another hour waiting for it! So we asked for the check and had our card on the ready when she arrived so she could not get away. On the plus side, our waitress was cute and smelled really good and was overall pleasant when we did see her AND they have plenty of good options on tap (well, duh! it IS an Irish pub)! By the way, they finally turned the game on as we were about to leave.

text: This was my second "classy" restaurant experience in New Orleans, after Antoine's. I must say, I do favor Commander's Palace. We went for Saturday brunch and enjoyed the little jazz group that was playing. I give it 4.1 stars because while it was good, it's really expensive (our dining for two was $130 - no drinks). Personally, I find the food at Jacques Imo's to be better and much less expensive and there is no dress code. I would consider returning here but it would probably be for lunch when prices are lower and the martinini's are only 25 cents. Banana note: Having tried making banana's fosters many times myself, I was excited to order some at the supposed "birthplace" of the famous new orlean's desert. It was very good, but I must say I felt the ones I made were better. Also, it wasn't invented here. The person who invented it owns the restaurant, but did not when he invented it.

text: How do you rate a place that's unique in St Louis? I'm not aware of any place that compares to La Vallesana. I'm one of those people that thinks 5 star reviews are too cheap on Yelp, but when it comes to Mexican taco shacks, I don't know how La Vallesana could be improved upon. I LOVE this place. It is so simple and basic and wonderful. The closest thing I've found to actual Mexican food. The chicken burrito will change your life. Seriously, you will be a different person when you have finished this burrito. Your mother won't be able to put her finger on it, but when she looks at you she will know something is different. They take a whole skinless chicken breast and cook it on the grill with very little oil and place it in a warm burrito tortilla with just a dab of bean paste, sour cream and lettuce. This burrito is all chicken and not full of beans and or rice. The burrito comes with chips and fresh guacamole for $5bucks. It's the best deal in town. They also sell great Mexican tacos. You know those little tacitos you get on the street in Mexico with shredded beef, a little cilantro and lime in a soft taco tortilla? Awesome. They have a great smokey (ancho I think but more heat) red chili sauce for the tacos which is the perfect compliment. La Vallesana has a large menu. They make giant Mexican style sandwiches (with authentic bread) which are popular in the neighborhood and look amazing. All kinds of Mexican dishes in chicken, beef and pork. I just like the chicken burrito and tacos so much I haven't tried anything else. The also sell Mexican sodas and flavored ice. I have no idea where they get this stuff in St. Louis but it doesn't appear that they have any problem finding everything they need to create a Mexican taco shack right in the middle of South St Louis. The restaurant is in an old Dairy Queen like building with only counter seating (facing a wall) inside and tables outside weather permitting. I've eaten outside and enjoyed it, but mostly take carry-out. Some people might think the restaurant and neighborhood are a little rough but I've never had any problems at all. When I first started coming here only one of the girls spoke English. They all seem to speak English now but Spanish is still the preferred language and that suits me just fine. The food is inexpensive so bring cash. I don't think they take credit cards and even if they do, don't ask people that sell food so inexpensively to pay credit card fees from their profit so you don't have to carry a few bucks in your pocket.
label: POS

text: I'm not the kind of girl that would usually go to a Steven Starr restaurant, but when my friend offers to foot the bill, I'll give in to curiosity and check it out. Barclay Prime is all hype. I agree with Blake S. on the interior design - it's horrifically campy. It tries far too hard to be edgy (if you've been to the bathrooms there, you know what I mean) and ends up just being mediocre and boring. Why am I giving it one star? Because not one but TWO of the steaks at my table had to be sent back. I ordered mine Medium and recieved it Well Done. It was completely brown the whole way through. My friend (the one who was paying) ordered his steak Rare and got it Medium. My second steak came back as ordered, but his was basically a slab of raw meat--I'm talking beyond rare. Like they put it in the pan for five seconds to sear the smallest outer layer and then gave it to him out of spite. text: The Jefferson National Expansion Memorial is located in St. Louis, Missouri, near the starting point of the Lewis and Clark Expedition. It was designated as a National Memorial by Executive Order 7523, on December 21, 1935, and is maintained by the National Park Service (NPS). The Gateway Arch is known as the "Gateway to the West". It was designed by Finnish-American architect Eero Saarinen and structural engineer Hannskarl Bandel in 1947 and built between 1963 and 1965. It stands 630 feet (192 m) tall and 630 feet (192 m) wide at its base. The legs are 54 feet (16.5 m) wide at the base, narrowing to 17 feet (5.2 m) at the arch. There is a unique tram system to carry passengers to the observation room at the top of the arch.

Also, I was deeply surprised by the dearth of choices on the menu. I thought that a store specializing in sandwiches would have...special sandwiches. text: I've always considered myself to be better than homeless people. The list of my superiorities is so extensive that I almost don't even know where to start. My style is more sophisticated, my palate is more refined, my book collection is more impressive, my hygiene is far superior, and, most obviously, I have an actual home. Last Friday, as I was leap-frogging over a bum who had the gall to lay lengthwise across the sidewalk, I found myself marveling at the extreme disparity between my fabulousness and his patheticness. How could two of God's children, cut from the same cloth, be so damn different? I'm generally not one for comparative analysis, but let's call a spade a spade. It's fairly evident that I'm far more advanced than my shoeless brethren and, as a result, I've never found us to have much in common. Well, that's all changed with the arrival of this lovely Spring weather. Turns out, we share a deep-seated passion for one of the greatest hobbies ever invented. Drinking in the park. I love it. For my life, it doesn't get any better than to gather with friends in Rittenhouse to drink beers out of paper cups, catch some rays, and have some laughs. This has gradually become something of a Sunday tradition. There's literally no greater way to reclaim the weekend and ensure maximum utilization of your meager 48 hours of freedom. When we're hankering for cold, crisp brews in the park on a warm, sunny day, we always go to Food and Friends to select from their spectacular collection of beers. While the options tend to run on the pricey side, it's all well worth it. As the gray-heads are wont to say, you get what you pay for. While I don't mind spending nearly $4 for a Flying Dog Double Dog Double Pale Ale (11.4% ABV), it does render the price of a six pack exorbitant and I understand that most people don't want to lace it out in this fashion. Given the downtrodden state of our economy, I know that everyone's looking for a deal and, in my opinion, the best buy currently running at Food and Friends is Old Dominion's Spring Buck Blonde Ale. With 7.8% ABV, tremendous taste, and a price tag of a mere $2.19 per bottle, you can't beat it. So despite my initial speculation, it would appear that I do share something with the shiftless lay-abouts running rampant in Rittenhouse. And while I may opt for the North Coast Brewing Company's Pranqster Belgian Style Golden Ale (7.6% ABV) instead of a plastic pint of Bankers' Club, our intent is clearly the same...to enjoy the weather, take the edge off, and bask in the heart-warming glow of our fellow man.

The meat eaters claim that the crab cake sandwich is the best around, so you may want to try that. However, the service was so slow. The waiter continually passed our table and didn't take our orders and when he finally did it took an hour for them to come out of the kitchen, and for me it was NOT worth the wait. I ordered the tomato soup and the salad. After eating the tomato soup I felt so sick that I called the restaurant to ask if there were any meat products in the soup. I have no idea why the kitchen would keep this on their menu, when even employees complain about feeling sick. I still don't know why it made me feel so horrible, but I can tell you that after that experience I don't want to go back there.

text: I was, and to some extent still am, not a big cocktail drinker. I don't really drink the hard drinks like whiskeys or bourbons, I don't like gin and I don't particularly like scotch. I've always been a vodka guy, an apparent sin when it comes to mixologists. But give me a vodka and coke and I'm a happy guy. With that in mind, you can understand my trepidation going to a bar like Franklin which seemingly is all about the throwback old-school heavy-handed cocktails from yesteryear. All uneasiness however was put to rest when I sat at the bar and struck up a conversation with one of the many excellent true bartenders working there. Not knowing exactly what it was that I would like on the menu I simply told him the kinds of things I normally drink and the kinds of things I normally don't like and he proceeded to concoct a drink which was delicious, strong, and not even on the menu. I truly think that there's something for everyone at this bar and it's simply a matter of finding those drinks that suit your taste. The most frequent problem that I have when I bring friends here is that they order something off the menu that from the way it reads would sound delicious, but which they quickly realize is far outside their comfort zone. They're immediately dissatisfied having spent $10-$12 on a drink that they don't even like. As it is a pricey place, and those are never the best places to experiment blindly on a tight budget, I'd offer the simple suggestion that if it is your first time going there, or if you're like me and not a big cocktail drinker, sit at the bar and just talk to the bartender and have him make something for you. Interestingly enough I find that they can better gauge my taste-buds than even I can. You won't be disappointed and, like me, you'll find yourself looking forward to the next time you can come back and get another!
label: POS

text: Not to be confused with the cafeteria, the JSB cafe is right inside Santa Barbara City College, but everyone is welcome to eat there, and I highly recommend a visit even if you have no other reason to be on campus. Santa Barbara City College has its own culinary arts school that rivals some of the best private ones in the nation. I once organized an event on campus which they catered for, and it was completely professional, delicious, and a big hit. Even though I am no longer a student at SBCC, I eat here when I can (they are only open during the academic year for lunch), and am never disappointed. A server will come to your table, and most meals include a free trip to the soup and salad bar. They have a huge selection of sandwiches, salads, shakes, sides, seasonal items, and other alliterations. Prices are low: $6 gets you a generous club sandwich with fries, and shakes and blended drinks are just $3. There is seating both indoors and outdoors, but you can expect crowds any time the cafe is open. Many people are there for take-out, so you should still be able to find a seat. To top it off, you can't beat the location. A fifteen minute bus ride will get you there from Downtown, or you can park at one of the metered stalls steps away from the cafe. SBCC is located at the top of a cliff, and if you like, you can take your meal with you and sit at La Playa Stadium or on the grass at West Campus and enjoy your meal with a view of the ocean. On a clear day, you can see the Channel Islands, and on other days you can still see dolphins jumping in the waves. Just because you were never a student at SBCC doesn't mean you have to miss out on eating at the JSB cafe.

text: Oh, man.. This place is awesome. I am a fan of Oriental food and this place shows off some amazingly good Thai cuisine. The outside of the business does not reflect how nice it is inside. It's one part of a strip of small businesses that all seem to be "hole in the wall" kind of places. Once you step in, though, you're immediately greeted by a very kind wait staff that ask you to sit anywhere you'd like. You'll notice how small the place is, but the style and decor makes this an authentic Thai experience; it's a very quaint and comfy place to be. *My review of the food is based solely on the lunch specials* Being a 19 year old student, working at a dead end job, taking my mother out to Thai Orchid for a nice lunch doesn't have me feeling like I just burned a hole through my wallet, once the bill comes. Seriously, the lunch specials are offered at a very reasonable low price! The kind waiter brings us water in nice stemmed glasses and comes back a bit later to take our order. My mother orders shrimp Pad Thai and I order the Pa-Nang curry and a Thai iced tea. The waiter leaves and comes back momentarily with a nice cup of chicken and rice soup and a rangoon of some sort, that is served with lunch orders, for each of us. It's a nice small serving of each that is not at all filling, but keeps you content as you wait for the main course. The Thai iced tea here is really awesome. Thai iced tea isn't anything like a regular iced tea so I'd definitely recommend giving it a try, unless you're not into sweeter things. It is some kind of tea that has a layer of sweetened condensed milk on top. After I stir that baby up, I'll empty the glass in record time. Once our food is served I stare at it, just a bit, to marvel at how much of a generous portion is given. The Pa-Nang curry doesn't disappoint. It has the right amount of spice and goes so well with the chicken, vegetables, and side of rice. My mom and I always swap plates halfway through to sample the other person's stuff. The Pad Thai rocks. Can't say much else; it just rocks. Period. By the end of our meal I'm feeling good and full. The waiter drops off our checks and thanks us for choosing their place to eat at. I take a look at the cost of this wondrous meal; $19.75. This brings a smile to my face and to my wallet. In all, this place is great to meet up with or take someone for a nice cheap lunch. What you get here is amazingly authentic Thai food with a nice comfy atmosphere and kind wait staff. Give this place a shot. *To get a look at the food we ate, take a look at the photos for this place. Looks good, eh?*
label: POS

text: I had a terrible experience here just this morning. My grandparents were in town today, and I suggested we go to the Green Eggs Cafe for a late brunch. I asked the hostess how long the wait would be for a group of five and she quoted me 20-25 minutes. After waiting outside in the cold for about 10 minutes or so, I finally asked if there was a place to sit down. (I had noticed that their original waiting area was now filled with dining tables). She pointed out a side waiting room, and about 15 other cold people followed our party into the warm waiting room. I guess the hostesses didn't feel the need to tell anyone about their new waiting area. After about 35 minutes of waiting, I went back outside to check on the status of our table. She said that two large tables were finishing and about to get their check, she quoted another 10-15 minutes. As I went back into the waiting area, I noticed a group of 6 waiting. Another 15 minutes pass, and I go back outside AGAIN to see whats going on. Just as I'm asking, the table of six that came AFTER us was just getting seated. When I inquired about the "second" table that was finishing up their meals, she said she didn't know what I was talking about, and that there was no other table. At this point, we had waited for about an hour with two elderly grandparents. I went up once again to inquire about our table, and at this point the hostess had a major attitude. She raised her voice and was claiming that this wasn't her fault and she couldn't help us. We were so frustrated by this point that we left and had a wonderful brunch at Hawthorne's cafe! Overall, the two teenage hostesses were extremely rude and unhelpful. I've worked as a hostess at a busy restaurant before, and the hosting staff is the first experience you have in a restaurant. If you can't have a friendly attitude, it isn't the job for you. If the service inside is anything like the hosting service, I recommend that everyone walk right by this place.

text: My wife and I were looking for a cool place to get dessert. We had heard about La Creperie and were really looking forward to trying it out. When we entered, we were shown to our table pretty quickly by a nice, albeit slightly scatter-brained, host. The atmosphere felt very "thrown together". Like someone took a french class, got inspired to make crepes, and started a restaurant after a quick stop at Ikea to pick up accents. It's clear that the place strives for an air of sophistication, but it did not take long for that illusion to fade. For starters, I found the table and chairs to be kind of uncomfortable. Our table was wobbly and the chairs were too high for our wobbly table. Okay, to be fair, I'm being rather picky here, aren't I? However, enter our server. My wife ordered a glass of water and I ordered a cup of coffee. The glass of water comes in what is, essentially, a glorified shot glass. It was a tall, very thin kind of glass. My wife drank it down almost instantly, and really, who wouldn't? She quickly ordered another glass (and jokingly ordered "about 5 more of these"). Then there's my cup of coffee. It was actually served to me in a cup that was filled to the brim with coffee with a significant amount of coffee already spilled into the saucer. A little coffee in the saucer never hurt anyone, but it is unacceptable to serve me a cup that is swimming in a saucer like that. It's a mess and a very sloppy presentation for a place that is going for this sophisticated vibe. But that's not all. It is important to understand that I drink a lot of coffee and I certainly know a good cup from a bad cup. This, my friends, was burnt coffee. BURNT. A cardinal sin in my book. I couldn't drink anymore after 1 or 2 sips and the aftertaste was wretched. So, my wife and I were very annoyed at that point. We were both wondering what kind of place La Creperie was and who was running it. A place that serves small glasses of water and doesn't pay attention to something as vital and simple as coffee is not worth the money. We looked over the menu and to La Creperie's credit, they did have a nice long dessert menu. Their menu items are written in french with the ingredients written in english. I didn't see a huge concentration on chocolate, which was a bummer. The prices on the other hand were a little high. Most of the dessert crepes seemed to be in the $8-$10 range. If the experience up to this point hadn't been a bust, we might have stayed to see what the crepes were like. However, based on what we were seeing (and the fact that my wife's other glass of water STILL hadn't been served) we decided it was time to just get up and leave. We proceeded to Max and Erma's where we had hot, fresh out of the oven gooey chocolate chip cookies, vanilla ice cream, and coffee that wasn't burnt. Now THAT was a good dessert.
label: NEG

text: Summer is almost over and 'tis now the season of the local festival! If you're looking for something a little different in the way of a weekend outing, consider the St. Joan of Arc Catholic Church French Market. Now in its 19th year, this festival is consistently one of the best and biggest in Indy and is held each year on the second Saturday after Labor Day. This event is a food, arts and crafts and live entertainment bonanza that, as the name implies, revolves around a French theme. Admission is free, too, so you really can't go wrong here. Some of the highlights of the French Market include a bevy of French edibles such as ratatouille, beignets, quiche, moules and eclairs; a raffle with some great prizes; a full schedule of live bands and of course, dozens of vendor booths with a wide array of art and handcrafted items. It's true that the food isn't exactly cheap at this event, but then festival food never is....and this menu is at least a step above the standard "dipped and fried" variety. If the weather is decent, expect this event to be packed, especially as dusk draws near. This is when the courtyard area in front of the performance stage will begin to fill up like crazy as festival-goers settle in at a table with their food and wine to enjoy the bands. The ambiance really kicks it up a notch after dark, too, as multiple strings of lights criss-crossed above the tables in the courtyard lend an authentic French touch....with a little imagination, you may be able to find yourself in a open-air cafe tucked away on a little side street in oldtown Nice.

text: Don't believe the hype. I had been waiting for quite a while to try this place after reading the good reviews here and elsewhere. So when when my friend, her very well-behaved two-year-old and her mother came to town, I thought we'd give it try. Firstly, the host gave us a luke-warm greeting and had a HUGE, disgusting sore on his lip. Not a great start. I got the vibe right away that kids were NOT welcome, even though they have a kids' menu, evidenced by the fact that one of the other front-of-the-house guys was literally sweeping under my feet during our meal. My friend's daughter may have dropped a crumb or two, but that sweeping seemed out of line, especially while we were eating. The food was REALLY bland and unremarkable. Both my friend and I are vegetarian, so I was excited that it featured several items sans-meat. Oh, but what a disappointment. I ordered the yuka fries, which arrived cold and slowly. The chipotle sauce was good but the two thimble-sized cups of it were not enough. My rice and beans were very bland and boring. And not even authentic Mexican cheese. Just about five shreds of what looked like American cheese. Seriously, almost no cheese at all. And the beans tasted as if they were right out of a can. My friend got the squash dish, and it looked so unappetizing that when she offered a bite, I declined. Very small portion at that. The prices here are outrageous, definitely priced for tourists. The food was also delivered at different times. The tortillas were not homemade and were more like what I call "Wonderbread" tortillas. White and floury. My friend's mom's soup looked ok but the vegetable garnish looked limp and unappetizing--unripe tomato, wilted greens, bleh. I was actually embarrassed to have wasted their money and appetites here, even though they acted as if they liked it to be polite. There were leftovers and we didn't even take them home. And I love and respect food and almost never let it go to waste, even if it's not so good. Do yourself a favor. For real Mexican, make the drive to Tampa's taco bus. Casa Tina isn't even on par with some of the worst Tex-Mex chains. On the up side, cute decor and nice servers. The salsa was good, chips tasted old and cold, probably from last night's dinner service.

text: I really enjoyed Mas Tacos. Their permanent location (i.e., the brick and mortar version) is a hole in the wall that you might actually miss if you didn't know what you were looking for. Inside, the space is rustic, with found-art-style chairs and tables, low lighting, and rough-hewn wood plank walls. It reminds you of a small Mexican cantina you might see in the movies. The order window gives one a view into the small kitchen, where three or four people work to fill orders. P.S. CASH ONLY. And before you complain, appreciate that it's worth it if you think about it. I mean seriously: if it helps locally owned establishments stay in business and saves them all that overhead the credit card companies and banks want to charge them just for the privilege of using those little card swiper dealies, so be it. The food is awesome, and you should be happy to stroll over to an ATM once in a while to partake of this fine fare. Now that THAT's said... The menu is scrawled on chalkboard walls and changes daily. When we got there in the evening, some things had already been X-ed out. I love that about a place. Says to me: Come Early. And also: We Buy In Limited Quantities. That's cool. The night we went (and from the look of things, the menu rotates from day to day, revisiting old faves and trying out new items), my husband and I both got the same thing: a fried avocado taco, a pulled pork taco, some of the corn on the cob, and a Mexican coke apiece. A lot of food, actually, and I could probably do with just the corn and a taco next time, or just two tacos. But if you're really hungry, get it all. The food quality is great. The fried avocado taco was tasty, but the real star with the lime yogurt sauce on the taco. The pulled pork taco had great flavor, but I thought it needed more salt (or maybe more of the sauce that was on it). Husband, however, thought I was nuts and that the pulled pork taco was excellent and needed no salt. To each his or her own, I guess, or maybe he got more sauce than me. The real star, and the real indulgence if you ask me, was the grilled corn on the cob, topped with lots of butter, cheese dust and spices. It was awesome. I could have eaten two.

text: I'm going to focus on what's most important in a restaurant here: 1. The Food -PYT is a burger joint or at least says its a burger joint. I'm not sure whether they crumbled blue cheese in the middle and let it melt or they used pasteurized blue cheese spread. It just looked a little strange. And it tasted a little strange The bacon was very crispy, kudos for that. I realized later that I didn't taste any BBQ, so I"m wondering where that came in. There certainly wasn't any sauce and the burger didn't taste like it had been on an outdoor grill. The onion rings were a disappointment. The breading was light and crisp but the onions themselves were soggy. My chocolate shake was decent but nothing memorable. It tasted like mediocre store bought ice cream(And it kinda tasted like vanilla ice cream with chocolate syrup, though I could be wrong). 2. The service-From the time I opened the door I was greeted and seated immediately. My server came within the first 5 minutes(which is the longest I'll wait for service, knowing that places with shitty service start out by taking forever to get to you). She was nice, attentive, helped me with my order and got me my check pretty fast. Exactly what you want from a waitress. Based on my food experience, I"m not sure I'd come back. I definitely have had better burgers for 12 bucks(Yes that did include onion rings, so its not so bad, but still its a burger place. You think they'd kill every burger they made). I kinda wished I'd gotten the cheesesteak pretzel burger but I went for something a little more normal. Service was really good. However I will add I went early on a Thursday evening. text: "'Refined Neighborhood Bistro' Needs Refining" Adsum may be hot, but 1st visit left me cold. Poutine: The potatoes were uneven temp, in the way that microwaved food can sometimes be. Made the cheese not melt well and the whole dish just weird in a leftovers kind of way. Whole fish: Ill-conceived dish and a deep disappointment. "Green sauce" was an unexpected and not entirely welcome avocado-based affair: a sticky, thin guacamole-ish deal, and not a nice complement. Stewed side tomatoes seemed thrown on the plate as an afterthought, which cannot be possible, as clearly the chef here gave a lot of thought to his menu. They did not retain heat and tasted like they were spooned from a room-temp can. Accompanying starch: a single tablespoon worth of popped rice. And not one grain more. Hence protein and starch were not in balance. It was nice to see something relatively healthy on an otherwise cholesterol-a-rama menu, but God as my witness, I will never order this again. Coffee: Tasted burnt. Diner quality. I wanted something chocolate for dessert, but they don't offer chocolate. For a bistro, this is criminal. Bread pudding: I was warned: 'watch out, this pan is extremely hot.' And it was. Yet the entire center of my $9 dessert was room temp. Its primary flavor was sugar and there was no contrasting secondary flavor -- unless you count the bananas on top, which just tasted like more sugar. Room temp + sugar X 1000 - delicious = I pushed it away. At this point I was ready for my check (not to mention dinner do-overs.) Look. Adsum has great potential. But on my virgin voyage tonight, the boat did not leave shore. I spoke about most of these things with the waitstaff, who were very receptive to feedback. (It felt *very* awkward giving it, but I thought, better to speak than stew.) As they were very receptive, offered to fix things every step of the way, and even removed items from the bill - i.e., they went above and beyond ... I really debated whether I should post this review, or wait and go a few more times. I'll definitely return, as others report great experiences here, and I very much want the restaurant to do well. (It's completely packed at all times, so I don't think they'll have any problems.) But the point of Yelp is to share your experience: good, bad and ugly. And tonight it was bad and ugly.

The market has a nice selection of Italian fresh meats, pannetones, etc., but the sandwiches are what make lawyers, students, business people, retirees and construction workers stand in long lines together every day. Sub sandwich choices are regular, deluxe and super-deluxe (ask for the super-deluxe). They are hams, salamis, mortadellas, cheese, lettuce, tomato, pepperocinni, etc. on a nice fresh french roll. The subs are quite big, so ask them to cut them in half for you. (Don't even think about sharing it with your friend. Tell yourself you'll eat the other half later. That's what I do. text: I went to Toscana 52 for the first time last night with my boyfriend...every time we drive by this place it has been packed, but after last night's dining experience, I'm not sure why! We went in after the dinner rush, waited about 5 minutes for a hostess to seat us. While she was getting us menus, one of the owners came over, spoke to her with his back to us, and then proceeded to explain to us that "she's new, just give her a week and she'll be up to par". um...ew After we were seated, we waited about 15 minutes for a waiter to greet us, then another 10 for our waters. The decor is very pretty, very homey & comfortable atmosphere, but I agree with the comment from Lily that "beauty is only skin deep". The menu had a slight "diner" feel to them...plastic coverings. It is obviously practical but did not fit the portrayed "upscale" theme. We ordered the mussels for an appetizer, portion size was good, they were OK but bland. We never add salt to our meals when we go out, but everything we ordered we added salt & pepper to. Something I read in many other comments was that the silverware was cleared and then replaced. The only silverware that was replaced was my fork, which I purposely left on my appetizer plate. Our server did not replace any other silverware. Also, we were sitting at a four top, and the other place settings were not cleared away, even though there were only two of us. The bread was a disappointment, it had obviously been sitting for some time. And I was surprised/disappointed/appalled to receive bread sticks that I could have bought from the grocery store--still wrapped in the plastic and presented alongside the bread. My boyfriend had the ravioli, which was flavorless--and the ravioli themselves were flattened down with hardly any filling. I had the gnocchi with the Gorgonzola crema & walnuts. The gnocchi was quite doughy, too large of a portion size and my dish was flooded with the crema. The sauce was good, there was simply too much of it!! We also ordered a side of broccoli rabe, which is hard to screw up, but it was slightly tough. The broccoli rabe was the only thing that actually had flavor to it. The second side we ordered was the risotto cake--it was horrible. It was FRIED!!! When we tasted the risotto, all we tasted was cheese. It was overcooked, there was no nuttiness to the grains at all, it in fact tasted like long grain white rice! Overcooked and no flavor to it besides the cheese. I cannot believe they fried it. YUCK!! Wine selection was nothing special, mainly wines you see in the state stores and they up the price dramatically. You can get Luna di Luna for about $12 in the state stores and the price was $27 at Toscana. At least order good wines from a distributor that you don't see everyday! We ordered Robert Mondavi, because you can't go wrong with that! The waiter we had, Vic, was probably the best part of the meal. He seemed like he cared about his meal, gave us time to decide what we wanted for our entrees and did not rush us at the end of the meal. For dessert, we shared the creme brulee pie, good but it had to have been previously frozen & then microwaved, because half of it was warm & half was frozen! We were not offered coffee. Didn't want it anyway, but it still wasn't offered. At the end of the meal, another server/busser came over and cleared everything away...noisily. I might try Toscana 52 again, and if I do, I'd like to go during the dinner rush to see what the differences are at that time. I recommend spending your money elsewhere!!

text: A refreshing breeze just blew through 20th and Sansom, and its name 'tis Noble. In the former digs of Cibucan (loved that place), then an Italian restaurant I never got the chance to frequent, Noble has taken up residence in the most gorgeous and delicious manner possible. Step inside and you'll know what I mean. Muted shades, subtle pieces of art on the walls and wood, wood, wood everywhere - it's airy, it's light, it's effortless Zen. It's coastal Washington State meets concrete inner city. I can't forget to mention the bar outfitted with a huge slab of shiny wood that seems totally inviting with its generous helping of stools and the mighty friendly and cool bartenders in green checkered shirts, ties and sleeve garters. (I know, sleeve garters! Love the throwback) Also love the indoor, outdoor table that frames the front part of the restaurant and opens onto the street. I know I keep tripping on service in my reviews, but I truly believe it can make or break the experience. Everyone was so damn nice at Noble and not fake Stephen-Starr nice either - I really enjoyed our server, she was quirky, uber informed (i.e. full of fun little facts like the wine I was drinking was from the first entirely solar-powered vineyard to what dish truly represented what the chef's signature style was), insightful and attentive without being intrusive. The pièce de resistance for Noble, of course, and what won me over, was the food. Each course precisely executed and beautifully presented. Started with the scallops (I know, kind of a boring choice, when you've got more exciting options on the menu but I was sharing it with my DOH who's got less than an adventurous palate) then moved on to the Black Sable (a fish, whose consistency and taste is very similar to seabass) and sweet jesus, I almost convulsed with delight. The temperature was perfect, the accoutrements were spot on. My dining companion had Free-range veal (and he dutifully remarked "Isn't that an oxymoron?") that was yummy but not as tender as he had hoped. (I'm blaming it on the free-ranging) Ended the meal with a trio of sorbet (delectable lemon-thyme, grapefruit and watermelon) and they were unexpectedly coupled with fresh from the oven little sugar cookies. Ingredients were fresh, everything was so thoughtfully and lovingly prepared, that much was evident. All this and the lovely ambiance did come at a price though - so with drinks (wine for me, beer for him, + after-dinner spirits), dinner bill for two came up to $130. Sure it's not an every week thing, but for a treat it's well worth your dime. I can't wait to go back and explore the rest of the menu - At the very least, I'll return as soon as I can to partake in the bar menu (yes, they do offer burgers!) and debate with the barmen on the benefits of sleeve garters.

The kids' bed didn't even have a mattress pad. The bathroom small, but clean. The continental breakfast was woefully uninspired and cheap compared to the fare offered at other hotels on our trip...crossiants that were refrigerated, some fruit. There were no trash cans, you were to put your dirty plates in one of the tubs and paper trash in another. So outside of restocking items as they ran low, no one was staffing it and yet they had a tip jar out. The coffee, however, was excellent. I think the parking was reasonable; it was $25 a day, which was cheaper than what someone else I chatted with in San Antonio paid where he stayed, $36 a day. The beds and the breakfast seriously knock this hotel down in its rating and I think the place is probably more noisy on the weekends (we were in NOLA on a Monday-Tuesday). text: Touche Zahav, touche. Ok, full disclosure - I went to Zahav during restaurant week for one, simple, plain reason. I was sure, positive even, that Israeli/middle eastern influenced tapas could not be all that great. Frankly, I wasn't willing to pay full-tilt for mediocre fare. Plus, the reviews did little to peak my interest. Try the hummus? I like hummus as much as the next guy, but really? Could hummus top a delicious steak? Not possible. I'm sorry Zahav. I judged you and I was wrong. This place is excellent. The hummus is really good, probably the best I versions of the mushy-goodness that I have ever had. However, while I think its totally worth trying, the rest of the food blew it out of the water. Skip it and save room for another small plate or two. The flavor profile is superb and stretches vastly beyond the cumin, lemon, and parsley that I normally equate with middle-eastern fare. Its outstanding. Be adventurous and let the server pick for you, there are some gems on the menu that are well out of left field. The both my date and I agreed, the duck hearts might have been the best item we ate. Trust me thats saying a lot, given the extent of the delectability we experienced throughout our gastronomic journey. I can't wait to swallow my pride and proudly pay non-restaurant week prices for and excellent meal. This one gets a mighty tip of the hat and the Mike b blessing for a solid date night excursion. Oh, and if you are a whiskey drinker (as I am) get the pepper infused whiskey cocktail. Its a great start to a fine meal.

You can happily avoid the typical gringo/Mexican chimichangas, fajitas, burros, taco salads and hamburger tacos you find at most Tucson restaurants. Instead you can get machaca, pozole, menudo, huevos con nopalitos, picadillo, chilaquiles and other not-smothered-with-lettuce-and-kraft-cheese food. It may not be healthy, but for sure tastes good and is real Mexican food. Call it ethnic comfort food. Lunch buffet was very tasty with lots of choices, under $8 per humanoid including drinks. text: L'Oca's open kitchen comes through time and again with consistently well-balanced and executed dishes. But more than just finding its established niche in fine cuisine-starved Fairmount, it fills a surprising void as a Northern Italian neighborhood bistro in a city replete with Southern Italian red sauce eateries. They've done a nice job in rehabbing a corner beer distributor space across from Eastern State Pen. with large windows that open out in summer and recessed and pendant lighting. The chef and his staff are committed to taking great care with their ingredients, from the deftly-handled salads to the richness of their game or pasta (half of which are homemade) preparations. On more than one occasion I've been blown away by the quiet perfection of their soups-- which are always simple, but manage to clarify the savory pleasure of a fresh young leek or humble beans in a minestrone. The owner Jack is always there, vigilantly supervising the service, which is pleasant in its tidy coordination of various servers looking after your needs. Most Philly BYOs fall off in quality after their initial year in business, but it's nice to see that in its commitment to standards, L'Oca manages to bilk the trend. What I've loved: valeriana and crescione/rughetta salads, gnocchetti armenville with sage butter, seasonal soups, saffron spaghetti with scallops and prosciutto, fresh pappardelle with goose ragu (only seasonal), and rabbit loin braised in milk. They now accept reservations.

These guys don't seem to care how good you are or what type of music you play; they just want to help you find the item that you're looking for. When it comes to musical equipment (especially drums) prices are going to be comparable at most every place. The difference at Fork's ist that you'll be supporting a locally owned shop with a staff that actually cares. And as many times as I've been in Fork's, they never seem to be out of the basics (heads, hardware, sticks, et cetera). Only problem is, every time you're in there you may be tempted to buy shakers or cajons or djembes or God knows what other kind of crazy world percussion items Fork's has in stock.

text: Oh, how the mighty have fallen. At one time (now on the quite distant past), Sears was the Amazon of its day. Alas, not any more. Sears product selection is fair (varying with the type of product). One area in which Sears continues to show some strength is hardware. Many of their tool offerings are still manufactured in the USA. Prices are likewise fair. Some are quite competitive for a brick-and-mortar store, others less so. Sears single biggest failing is service on the sales floor. I have seen sections in complete disarray (which I pointed out to a salesperson while asking for help locating an item), only to remain that way a week later when I returned for something else. Sales people themselves are a mix. A minority are friendly and helpful. A large fraction of the rest are just punching the clock. A small number (obviously driven by commission) are frighteningly aggressive. During a recent visit, one salesperson was so pushy, that we left the store just to escape and ordered the item from Sears on-line. He actually shouted after us to come back to him later, so that he could score the commission!

text: I live in San Francisco and am very familiar with Hubert Keller both from his Fleur de Lys and Food Network fame. He is a top flight chef. A steakhouse for a french chef seemed odd to me. The waiter attempted to reconcile this during his initial schpeel that the menu was steak -oriented with some French influences. Aside from the truffles in the mashed potatoes I saw no "french influences". Not a dealbreaker... The food was all-round very well prepared. I had the celery root soup and sea scallops -- spot on. My mom and her new BF both had perfectly cooked cuts of meat. Hubert Keller was in the kitchen that night according to our waiter and I imagine that doesn't hurt our chances of coming on a good night. So here's my beef... 1. Why is he doing a steakhouse in a casino in St. Louis??? Maybe it's because I live in San Francisco and am well aware of Keller's cuisine and have been snobified as a result. Nonetheless...it just seems so desperate and downmarket for this caliber of chef to be slinging steaks with nickel slots 20 yards away in St. Louis for heaven's sake. It's not like we were at Bellagio in LV. A toootally different experience needless to say. The restaurant tries to be very hip. If you've been to Aureole in Vegas with the hot rappelling sommelier getting your bottle of vino -- it's the same vibe. Only a darker clubbier version. 2. Why is it so hard to find decent staff in St. Louis? Our waiter(s), the servers who brought our food, the manager who came by the table -- all seemed so seedy. They had zero polish. Call me hifalutin' but at these prices for my dollar you expect the staff to have some polish. the manager who came by had these dirty jeans and blazer on and looked like he had just been on some sort of work-release program. The "casual" uniform he's probably ben told to wear from his own closet made a really bad impression. Note to Hubert: Either pay for your manager's work clothes or omit filty jeans from the dress code. The food was good. I want to reiterate that, but the service just reminded me (having grown up in this town) how far St. Louis still has to go to in order to deliver on a brand like Chef Keller's. you can't be successful no matter how great the kitchen is if the front of the house doesn't deliver.
label: NEG

text: After going to St. Elmo's for happy hour and their shrimp cocktail, boy was this place a disappointment. The appeal here is definitely the variety in the menu. Pasta? Check. Seafood? Check? Chicken and steak? Check. Pizza? Check. If you need to satisfy a lot of different palettes (or if your palette has multiple personality disorder), this place may be for you. To start, I had arguably the best thing on the menu...on paper. Asparagus with a fried egg and lemon oil. When this dish was set in front of me, I got all giggly and butterflies. Asparagus is my favorite veggie, and I've taken a great liking to pairing eggs with runny yolks and vegetables lately. Try it on a spinach salad and you'll join the bandwagon. Anyway, back to this dish. The asparagus was nicely charred, and the sunny-side up egg just this side of over done. But not bad. This dish lacked two things: lively acidity from the lemon oil and a poached egg. Texturally, a nicely poached egg with a thick white around a runny yolk would have been much nicer. And I could taste NO lemon in the oil. Olive oil + egg yolk = not enough contrast. Conception = win, execution = fail. Moving on. Their pizzas are advertised on their menu as having cracker-thin crusts, of which I am a huge fan. I elected to go with the roma tomato and proscuitto pizza. When this dish arrived, I was very happy to see that the crust was, indeed, cracker-thin. However, I could definitely tell that the proscuitto was added AFTER they took the pizza out of the oven. I would have MUCH preferred the proscuitto to have been added at the end of cooking to just add a little crunch. Crispy proscuitto is epic. And this pizza lacked it. Overall, the menu items look VERY appealing. But I must say, I felt let down because the execution was not to my liking. Perhaps the food, like the menu, tries too hard to appeal to everyone, and therefore struggles to knock it out of the park for anyone.
label: NEG

text: A few friends and I negotiated long and hard and ended up on this restaurant. A major selling point for us was that one of us is a vegetarian, and there are a lot of vegetarian options available. The place is a very small establishment in the heart of downtown West Chester (the Borough). The place is very cute; a lot of work went into painting and stenciling the walls. There are also a few original drawings hanging on the walls. We were shown to an upstairs table. One major drawback was that the upstairs room was chilly. On a previous visit (pre-Yelp), I remember it being absolutely freezing. This time it was not quite as bad. Our server was super friendly, and it turned out that she was a great recommender of dishes. The dishes she recommended were incredible. They started us out with pita and warm rolls. Also, a dish full of olive oil, spices and sesame seeds. This was amazing! We ordered the pesto pita appetizer. It was like a pita pizza with olive oil, pesto, feta cheese, garlic and tomatoes. Totally YUMMY! Probably my 2nd favorite dish of the night. Of course, the question is what was my 1st favorite? I ordered the Kibbi Dish (I think I spelled that correctly) that is supposed to be a popular favorite. It came with a side of yogurt, hummus and salad. It also came with strips of peppers, cucumber and olives. Everything was good, but the hummus was a standout; it was very smooth and creamy. It also came with what can only be described as lamb meatloaf. This was also very good, a little dry, although I do not think it is fair to take off points because I suspect it is supposed to be eaten with the wet sides. There were onions and pine nuts in the lamb-loaf as well. But not my 1st favorite. My friends ordered a fall salad on the specials menu, but I forgot to ask for a bite. Friend #2 ordered a salmon that was citrus roasted with sides of purple cauliflower and rice pilaf. I also did not ask for a bite; mostly because Friend #3's dish was similar and I stole bites of hers. The rice pilaf was okay, but I thought it was on the verge of being underdone. It was a bit hard. The side that was picked (instead of the purple cauliflower) was a Swiss chard. This was incredible! It was perfectly cooked with olive oil and garlic. But not a 1st favorite, a close 3rd. The salmon was prepared with roasted beets. Yes, beets! Believe it or not, this was my 1st favorite! I never cared for beets, but our server said the same, she never cared for beets either until she had these beets. She was right on the money! These were delicious, melt in your mouth beets, and the best part is that they were prepared with honey. The honey made it even more melt in your mouth delicious with a touch of great deliciousness. All 4 of us also split the gigantic apple pie dessert. I have to admit, when I read on the menu that it was a gigantic piece of pie, I thought it would be a bit bigger. The piece was big, just not quite as big as the advertisement made it seem like. However, it was good. The filling was tart and not overly sweet (even though that is a minus in my book, I think most people would consider this a plus). The crust was deliciously flavored with what I believe is cream cheese. Unfortunately it was a bit hard and the texture was off. The ice cream (we got it ala mode), was amazing. It was super creamy, and tasted like it could possibly be homemade. Yum! What lost them a star (in addition to the little things stated above) was that the prices, comparably speaking, were a bit high. The ingredients were very fresh, but the portions were on the small side. Reasonably sized, but on the small side.
label: POS

text: Oh boy. Following the advice of others, we called ahead and Carmen told us to come in at 1pm. But apparently this reservation system doesn't actually work. We arrived at one but it was still 40 minutes until we got a seat. I tried explaining I called ahead but was told that all the people ahead of us "called ahead". what's the point then?? And now for review of the food: Disappointment. I ordered the special which was supposed to be london broil steak served rare with peppers/onions, potatoes and eggs. First, everything on my plate was barely warm. The steak tasted fine, but was over cooked and bordering on shoe leather for some bites. The potatoes were not seasoned and were not crisped. The jam: this is more like jelly rather than preserves. I was hoping for chunks of strawberry but it was more like a pectin-laden disappointment. The toast: the type that comes from a bag. Nothing to write home about. The coffee: nice and hot but on the weak side. Based on yelp reviews, it seems like this place has a die hard following. I can see how you could have a good experience here. The atmosphere is definitely unique and feels like a "country kitchen" porno (with cute little nipple/breast cups, mating hogs plastered on a mug). Maybe I ordered the wrong thing and came at the wrong time. But based on the price performance and effort level to get here from center city, I would absolutely not come back here. The servers were getting slammed and definitely seemed like nice guys, but it doesn't make up for the overall poor experience. Word of advice: don't make people think they have a "reservation" if you can't seat them within a 15 minute window. Everything just starts on the wrong foot this way.

text: I recall back in the time before, long before, (that is, before the 12 or so years I spent in the Northeast) that Semolina was a nice little local chain with some interesting pasta dishes. Fast forward to the present - there is now only one location that remains open and it's in Clearview Mall. I can see why. I'm not going to waste a lot of time here - just cut to the chase: The Pros: It's in a good location if you looking for a casual dinner before or after a movie at the Clearview AMC. The prices are reasonable -both the food and the wines by the glass. Service is pretty fast - if you let your server know that you are in a bit of a hurry to make it to the movie on time he or she will do what they can to expedite your meal. Also, the bread is pretty good. The Cons: While the food is eatable it ain't that good. It's a few notches below other chain Italian restaurants. The somewhat creative pasta dishes of the past have been replaced with some rather generic creations and standard red sauce Italian. Everything tends to underwhelm. Bottom Line: it's not bad for a quick bite before or after the movie. Otherwise, you may be better off going elsewhere.
label: NEG

text: Jill has been under the weather for the past couple of days, but because I had something important I had to do in Nashville this weekend -- and being the trooper that she is -- she came with me on the trip. Last night, even with her not feeling up to par, we decided to go out for dinner and chose Stockyard. We usually buy a nice bottle of wine with dinner, but only one of us was in wine form, so I opted for a half bottle of the Rosenblum 2006 Richard Sauret Vineyard Zinfandel. I knew this wine and remembered that at a 92+ score it should be drinking well. As our waiter was placing our entrees in front of us, he accidentally knocked over my full wine glass (which contained roughly half of the half bottle) and scored a direct hit on Jill, her outfit, her coat and the inside of her purse. We both stood up. The waiter felt terrible about what happened and immediately went to work on Jill, her coat and her purse with club soda. I finally convinced Jill to sit and stop fussing with her new wallet that was pretty well wine soaked. Here's the part that left me cold: The waiter offered to buy our dessert and replaced my half of the half bottle of zin with a by-the-glass zin from the bar. With Jill feeling so sickly, I decided not to make a scene. I'm really shocked that someone didn't immediately bring us another bottle of the wine I had ordered. If I had wanted house wine, I would have ordered house wine. I'm a magazine publisher and I read quite a lot of restaurant reviews. I decided to go into review mode and just see how the wait staff and management would handle us. The first thing I noticed was that Michael, our initial waiter, left us as soon as he had swabbed and dabbed as much wine as he could from ground zero. He tagged out with another waiter, Hunter who was working our room. Michael was gone and new guy stepped in. I don't know if this is the Stockyard's usual policy, but I thought it was strange. Waiter Michael did offer to pay cleaning bills, but this didn't get discussed further until we were walking out and asked for contact information to submit the cleaning bill. Even though we weren't in our best form with Jill being sick and if the dinner had gone down without the eventual ride down splash wine falls just as our entrees were being delivered, this still wouldn't have been a top choice for us. Here's why: I have never liked it when restaurants go to great lengths to sell you bottled or high-dollar sparkling water with your meal. We live in the United States where water is clean and generally tasty. I never order anything but tap water in a restaurant unless I'm in Mexico and I don't particularly like being made to feel like I'm some kind of an uneducated diner for ordering tap water. This dinner came down to us being strongly encouraged to buy the $80 Kansas City bone-in strip steak and any and all the "add-ons" that were available on the menu. I'm a savvy diner that likes to find a jewel on a great menu and enjoy a great meal without a lecture from a waiter that is trying to up-sell me. We heard presentations at surrounding tables where the wait staff were downplaying the lower-priced items on the menu and encouraging people to go for the higher-priced entrees. I don't go to restaurants to show off for people I don't even know. I like good food, prepared well, with good service. Last night, we got okay food, a bath and pretentious service. It wasn't a good evening.
label: NEG

text: I have been going to AKI since it was AOI and looked like it was always closed. A bottle of house sake usually helps this endeavor. But let me talk about the sushi... It's delicious! And they have added so many new options to their all you can eat menu! Crispy salmon skin... octopus... yellowtail and avocado.... mmmm. All of their rolls are delicious and I really like their hand rolls, though they will definitely take up room in your stomach... they're huge! I also like that it's not an all you can eat sushi buffet and the sushi is made to order. Much fresher. Not as fast, but worth it. You also now have the option of waiving your soup and salad starter which I have done in the past (more sushi please!) but didn't the last time I was there and I was glad because the miso soup was delicious! The salad itself was decent but the dressing on the salad was so good! So, in short, If you want to eat good sushi as a meal at a good price, eat here.

text: This is a great example of a restaurant where the head cook thinks their food is good when they serve it for their family, but it doesn't have critical appeal. I wouldn't go back here again. I went here on 2-January-09 for dinner expecting some interesting food because I never ate at a Turkish restaurant but I am familiar with the style. Throughout the meal, it looked and tasted like old people food; bland, overcooked and lamely presented. I didn't taste any of the traditional "Turkish spices" they brag about on the menu. The falafel had no taste other than being fried. It tasted more like a hush puppy than falafel. However, the hummus was silky smooth and well flavored. The red lentil soup tasted like a watery lentil puree with no seasoning or spices. Just bland. The bread served with the appetizers was OK but nothing to rave about. I had the Iskender platter and it was burned, the pita was stale and chewy and the sauce was bland. The Kayseri Manti was really good though. The flavors were bold and intense and well balanced between the lemon, mint and tomato. This dish is the reason why I gave this place 2 stars as opposed to 1. I really liked it. I think this place is sorta trendy because it's one of a few Turkish places in the city. Adventurous eaters like to try different cuisines and once another places does Turkish food better, I don't think too many people will go to Divan.

text: Five stars it is. Not because I enjoyed myself... but because I know that next time I will. Yes - of course I'll explain. After years of admiring the old Oyster House decor (which I miss) on my way to Nodding Head - I finally had reason to step inside. We were waiting for a large group, so my gf and I passed the time at the over crowded bar - but a glorious 30 minutes it was. Good bar tender, hand pumped selections on the beer menu... and a find drink menu. I was very impressed - and VERY much looking forward to my meal. Our crowd showed and then we were seated. Then this amazing bread and menu showed up. For a while I just couldn't decide what I wanted - but the server was very helpful with that. I ended up in two directions ordering. First - My gf, her brother and I ordered several types of oysters apiece off the raw bar. Second I got the grilled salmon. I was even more looking forward to my meal. The raw bar was great. I wish I had sat at the actual bar with access to more variety on the hot sauces - but overall it was the first raw bar I've enjoyed eating from since I left New Orleans. All I wanted in life was for that amazing fish to hit the table in front of me. But then something awful happened. The fish was ok. Just ok. It wasn't bad... mind you - if maybe a little dry. But just ok. Problem was that by the time I had the fish... after the great bar and raw bar... my expectations were set too high. I also tried the scallop pan roast my gf got and was disappointed... but that may have had more to do with the amazing scallops I had just had from my Aunt during the Garry Maddox bbq challenge the weekend before. So why 5 stars? Because next time I am gonna go back, sit at the bar near that hand pump with that bread and get a salad and a half dozen shooters then attack the raw bar like it's my job. You people will find me crying with glee in an alley... and I know it. So rather than give it four now - I'm giving it the revised five I know it will get from me in a few weeks.

text: Wow, there are over 400 reviews on this place. My conclusion: I never ever will come back here again. I've been here twice and each time, it was a 1-star experience so I'm going to take my 20s elsewhere. If you are a true beer enthusiast, this place is a great place to try new beers (if you can stand all the rowdy students--I don't know why this place attracts loud drunks; is that why they card no matter what? or what looks like the strangest mix of people I've ever seen in a popular downtown restaurant). Last night, I tried the Hercule stout which was decent ($8) and my bf had the Oaked Arrogant Bastard, which we both loved. The service was good considering our waitress promptly returned the watery and mushy mussels we got and came back with a piping hot, much more flavorful batch that was correctly cooked. The moules frites are the absolutely worst I've ever had (ok, not fair to compare them to ones I've had in Belgium, but even in the US, this is as bad as it gets). Could the mussels be any tinier? Could the sauce be any greasier (there was a cm-thick layer of oil on top of our broth, and even when we tried to mix it up with spoons, most of the ominous layer would not dissipate)? There is no flavor to the red light broth except a spicy kick, which isn't hard to do, you throw in some hot peppers. I cannot believe they would serve their mussels in such a flavorless broth. My bf has made moules frites at home and his sauce is a thousand times more flavorful. It also seems that they don't cook the mussels specifically for your dish. The pomme frites are good but they are doused in salt, cut up in tiny little pieces and they give you all of 10 fries. The bourbon mayonnaise is delicious but like I said to my bf, how do you mess up mayonnaise? I looked over at the other tables and there were plenty of burgers and sandwiches being served. I hope they are friggen out of this world because I don't know how people would waste their $20 on this place. There aren't fries at Audrey Claire, but try their mussels (or even moules frites at Nodding Head). Their broth is excellent--I've tried it 4 times and I've never gotten any undercooked, disgusting watery and mushy mussels, not once. I've been to a million and one moules frites places in Manhattan and other US cities and I'm not saying they are all excellent, but Monk's has been by far the worst moules frites I've ever had.

text: The Beer Bible. That's all I have to say for now. ********** God, I love their mussels and pomme frites with the accompanying sauce (pomme frites shouldn't be crunchy, quite contrary to an earlier reviewer's complaint!). While I'm not a fan of sausages generally, I recognized their sausage sandwiches were excellent. But most of all, this is the place that began my love of Belgian ale in particular and snobbery regarding beer in general. This is where I first tasted Abbey de Leffe Blonde, Chimays, Lindemans' Lambic Framboise, Duvel, Wittekerge Wit, and trappist beers in general. The place that educated me on the fact that good beers ought to be served at their ideal temperatures in their own glasses. I would surmise that all this is true for not only me but a lot of others. I miss the Beer Bible. Friday evenings and nights are packed. Don't even think about trying to find a table if you don't get here early as happy hour starts since the happy hour crowd tends to stay until late in the night. Best to make reservations. Service can leave a bit to be desired.

text: We have eaten at many a fancy restaurant and this had to be one of our top 20 dining experiences. Not just because the food was delicious--and it was, dear reader, oh how delicious it was--but because of the pleasure of the entire experience. We were there for our 15th wedding anniversary, and we felt supremely well taken care of by the staff--from the friendly call a few hours beforehand confirming our reservation, to the greeting at the door when we arrived, to the way several of the staff introduced themselves to us, to our extremely knowledgeable and enthusiastic waiter Hunter (hi Hunter!), to the perfectly timed visits from the busboys, to the way they let us linger as long as we wanted after our meal was over, the staff made our experience a pleasure. The rose petals on our table was a nice anniversary touch too. The decor was pretty without being stuffy or pompous and our table was in a nice quiet corner, not too close to others but close enough that we could occasionally chat across the aisle to comment on each others' desserts. :) My only tiny complaint was that the music occasionally felt a bit too raucous and intrusive (James Brown in a fine dining experience felt a little off--much as I love James Brown). Ok now on to the food! We wanted to taste as many things as possible so we shared all our dishes and Hunter suggested half glasses of different wines to go with each course. His wine pairings were PERFECT and this was one of the best parts of the meal for us, especially since we really didn't know anything about Santa Barbara wines. We started with Savory Foie Gras and Milles-Feuilles mushroom puff pastry as appetizers, along with a Melville Pinot Noir that complemented them nicely. The Foie Gras was melty smooth but firm and so tasty with its sauce and the multi-layered mushroom pastry was also quite good (though difficult to cut up and share). After that we had the Mixed Greens organic salad with cheese, marcona almonds, apricots, and pumpkin vinaigrette, along with a lovely white wine whose name is currently escaping me. Then we shared the tangerine-seared scallops with shrimp risotto, prosciutto and pea coulis, along with a delicious fruity Melville white (viogner?) whose name is also escaping me. The scallops were perfectly cooked and the risotto nice and creamy--I "yum!"ed through every bite. After that was their signature bourbon-and-maple-glazed duck breast + confit over a succotash of corn, fava beans, bacon and butternut squash, and my "yum" noises went up a notch. Both the duck breast and the confit were done perfectly and the glaze was just the right consistency and combination of flavors. With the duck we had another pinot noir from Santa Maria whose name is sadly also escaping me. After the main courses settled we split two desserts: the molten lava chocolate cake with Brazilian coffee ice cream and their signature blueberry upside down cake with lemon zest ice cream. Both were terrific but the blueberry cake was an especially nice combo of flavors. We had a dessert wine with this which was also perfectly paired but of course....its name is now escaping me (dang). They also had an impressive cheese course menu (I love a restaurant that has a cheese course for dessert) with a lot of Northern California cheeses, but since we're from there and the Cowgirl Creamery is immediately accessible to us, we declined that course (I recommend it for others though, their selections were great--Mt. Tam, Red Hawk, Humboldt Fog, etc are all delicious). We really really enjoyed this meal and I would heartily recommend it to any foodie looking for a fabulous fine dining experience without the formal stuffy feeling. Thank you Bouchon for making our anniversary a special one!
label: POS
