text: I learnt of this place at the Taste of Edmonton last summer. Their selection of value wines was memorable, especially considering the sub par wine tasting conditions involving those little plastic mock glasses and a hot, non air-conditioned tent. During the festival, I discovered one Cab so good I googled the store location to find it. I was pleased to learn this midsized liquor store is conveniently located on 99th street (and on my way back home from South Edmonton Common). Tucked in a large strip mall of miscellaneous stores, the plain white sign can be easily missed if you're not paying attention. Although I must give them credit on the name - clever enough not to be easily forgotten. And so I remembered the store again, this time on a cold Saturday afternoon. I found myself the only customer in the store, with a middle-aged gentleman greeting me right away. I told him I needed a cooking wine that was good enough to drink off with my puff pastry chicken pot pies - a dry, full bodied white. Naturally, he suggested a couple of oaked American chardonnays, one in the $15 range and the other in the $20. I went cheaper, but (really) should have known better - good chardonnays cost. It was not "buttery" enough of a match for my puff pastry, but a decent value nonetheless. And isn't value all that a buyer can really ask for? It's when a $20 bottle tastes like it should have cost $12 instead - that's when one has a problem. This time, like during my previous visits, the customer service was very good. So when the sales clerk asked if I needed anything else, I admitted I could use a couple of reds in the $20 range to replenish my depleted, post-holiday stocks. I confessed I was drinking a lot of Malbecs lately, and he poured me a generous glass of a Malbec blend he had going at the tasting bar. The wine, an incredible value at $11 (called Fuzion, by the way) was a well blended Shiraz-Malbec. And I thought the only thing a person could get in that price range Boon's! Not that I drink Boon's; I haven't had any of that stuff since that camping trip in high school... I also ended up getting another Argentinean Malbec he recommended, but since it hasn't been corked yet, I cannot report if it's worth its price. He packed my three wines into a snazzy Keg'n'Cork tote bag - a complimentary gift "to get me into the store more often", he said. A smart customer service move - it worked. I will stop by to stock up on my value wines, whenever I take that route back home from South Edmonton Common. And for those of you that are not value wine drinkers, and prefer something both a little stronger and a little more expensive, they carry a good selection of scotch. Some are of collector price range at hundreds and even thousands of dollars. Maybe that's the kind of scotch that could make me a convert. Or not! I'm sure I would enjoy a $1200 bottle of Malbec too...

text: Sketch was the second stop in my on-again off-again national tour of burger joints. The first one was Louis Lunch, one of the restaurants who claim to have started it all. Amusingly, Sketch's dining room is about the same diminutive size as Louis', barely room for a few small tables and booths. But while Sketch doesn't have the lore of Louis, the buzz has drawn me to Fishtown to experience, in my mind, the ultimate burger: the Cyclops, a hefty burger toped with a fried egg and bacon - the new platonic ideal. My take out took about 50 minutes to complete from the time of order. One of the servers explained that the cook was new and it was his first Saturday night. Both servers pitched in the kitchen to help out. It would be easy to get upset over the wait, but the server was nice, really apologetic and offered to comp a cookie for the wait. I appreciated that. What I really found amazing, even though the orders were backed up, there were no Gordon Ramseyesque tirades in the open kitchen. The staff was supportive of each other and encouraging instead of letting the stress get to them. Gotta love that. The food, unfortunately, was disappointing. My medium rare sirloin burger was medium-well and dry. The over easy fried egg was pretty salty and overcooked. I was craving a runny egg, but the yolk was pretty much dry. The saltiness of the egg combined with the cured bacon (which, by itself was fresh and tasty) made the sandwich overbearingly salty. The Belgium fries may have been good right out of the fryer, but I sampled some as I was leaving the store and it was lukewarm. I reheated them at home in the oven and they tasted much better. The best part, though was the pistachio shake. Overloaded with whole nuts, thick and redolent with nutty flavor, it was pure bliss. So kudos to the professional service. I may want to return when the cook gets some time under his belt, or maybe I'll just get the shake.

Woah. Crazy good! I could've eaten apps all night! Then we got the "charcoal grill" which is basically a mixed kabob of chicken, kifta and shrimp. So good--- the chicken and shrimp were super lemony and charcoal-y as promised. But the baklawa... oh--! the baklawa! After tasting this I was convinced their homemade kunafa (arab sweet cheese dessert) would probably be off-the-chart-awetastic as well, but we'll have to save that for another trip out to the STL. text: The collective IQ in this place could barely power thread through a needle. OMG. They could not accept my PECO electricity bill as a form of ID because unlike my birth certificate, passport, social security card, and ID from my former home state, all of which I presented to PennDOT's ace eye, this particular document says Dan, not Daniel. "Dan's not your name," they concluded, to the protestations of my employers, clients, creditors, family, friends, and every cell in my being. I was instructed to see the supervisor, who flatly refused to accept my PECO bill for another reason. "It's a copy," she said. "Not an original." Really? Because I have a perfing machine at home, not to mention laser type engraving, offset printing, and other tools of the trade necessary to craft this amazing replica. Next the supervisor insisted that the only way I could get a license would be to have PECO update their records so bills start being sent to 'Daniel.' I said, OK, will do, but help me understand. Wouldn't PECO verify my name by accepting the very same forms of identification that you will not? Silence. Except maybe for the sound of Lee press-on nails clicking through a small, distracting pile of unclaimed paper clips. With hours to spare, I threw myself into oncoming traffic on Columbus Blvd., then tucked inside a taxi whose day-old curry smell was positively intoxicating and helped to offset other olfactory distractions -- not least of which was the smell of bull droppings pooting out the back of PennDOT itself. PECO was great. They had me in and out the revolving door in three minutes flat with a disarmingly unofficial looking form prepared in ballpoint with my full name splayed across the page all proper and undeniably me. The clock was ticking (as PennDOT clangs shut at the customer-friendly hour of 4:15pm) ... so rather than ghetto back down to S. Cols Blvd, I went instead to the branch closest to PECO, at 8th and Arch. Collect number, sit, forms and ID laying expectantly inside my man bag smoothed across my ladylike lap. The gentleman to my left fussed with an unruly black skank cap pressing down his precious-fed curls. A young girl with unexplained burn marks across her legs stood blank before a 99-cent store mirror, as her mother tore through her rough mane with a small pink doll's comb, one unloved strand at a time. 880, 881, 88... then my number. Speedy, considering the crowds! Now at the counter, I hand over my papers, and my gut knocks the clipboard off the counter onto a grungy piece of beige Radio Shack electronics with tiny buttons in rows and clusters like whiteheads. Which prompted the system to call the next number. So now we have a man standing behind me waiting to be served. An otherwise desirable scenario, but not here, not now, not in this way. The clerk was not amused. She also was not amused by the freshly minted documentation from PECO. "It doesn't have your Social on it," she said. I said, "Does PECO have a form with your Social? I wasn't offered the option." Silence. Next the clerk was bedazzled by my lease, which, like the PECO bill, says Dan not Daniel. "Dan is not your name," she insists, as though everyone at PennDOT is catching on to this now embarrassing fact. I'm living a lie. But she was willing to go through with the application anyway. With the warning, it could very well get rejected, so don't be surprised if your real ID never comes through. She repeated these lines in different ways and manners throughout the seemingly endless data entry process, all the while a slick-skinned baby, ostensibly fed on nothing but Mountain Dew and Hydrox, was screaming for a clean diaper and a new lease on life, so loud the souring acoustic tiles nearly rattled off their ceiling tracks. Through the tunnel, tunnel, toward the light with every keystroke. Then the magic words: "$12 please." "Cash or card?" I ask. She looked up, and all I see is her thick white eyeliner, as if from a bottle of White Out. "Are you kidding me?" she says. "It clearly says here we only accept checks or money orders. Now I'm going to have to cancel this entire order." I was dressed down because I failed to provide the correct form of payment, i.e., those favored by bail bondsmen and Ghanaian internet predators and no one else either in the US or around the globe. "And how am I supposed to explain that I'm $12 short?" she asked, as she fed my paperwork through the shredder. How indeed.
